background: In November 2026, Europol and international law enforcement partners dismantled infrastructure supporting several malware operations . Among them was CastleRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) that enabled criminals to remotely control infected computers. Europol provided HIBP with 180k email addresses associated with CastleRAT infections, along with 893k unique passwords observed more than 3M times across accounts used on infected computers.
Later that month, Europol provided a further 251k unique email addresses and 1.3M passwords. The passwords from both datasets are now searchable via Pwned Passwords .
how: In November 2026, Europol and international law enforcement partners dismantled infrastructure supporting several malware operations .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 430,557 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: This entry is not a company that lost its customers' data. It is the other side of the transaction: a remote access trojan, taken down by Europol and its partners, whose infrastructure held what it had collected from infected computers. If your address is in here, the likely story is not that a website you trusted was breached.

It is that a machine you used, or one an account of yours was signed into, was under someone else's control. That changes the advice. Changing one password is the response to a site breach. A RAT sees everything typed on the infected machine, so every password used there should be treated as known, including ones for sites that were never breached at all.

The 893,000 unique passwords Europol shared are now in Pwned Passwords, which is the quickest way to check whether yours is among them. The order matters. Clean or replace the infected device first, then change passwords from a different, trusted device, starting with email, because email resets everything else. Changing passwords on a machine that is still compromised just hands over the new ones.

The record's dates are unusually tight. The takedown happened in November 2026 and the data reached HIBP the next day, because it came from law enforcement rather than from a criminal forum. That reverses the normal sequence in this archive.

Instead of finding out years after the data started circulating, people in this set can learn about the compromise around the time the operation was disrupted, which is the earliest anyone could reasonably have known. The numbers also say something about password habits.

Europol shared 893,000 unique passwords that were observed more than three million times across accounts on infected machines, which means many of those passwords were seen more than once. If you find one of your passwords in Pwned Passwords because of this entry, assume every account that shares it is exposed, not only the one you were thinking of.
A password manager that generates a different password per site is what stops one infected machine from becoming access to everything.

background: In October 2026, the Discord server protection service Double Counter suffered a data breach attributed to a vulnerability in the Metabase analytics tool . In its disclosure notice, Double Counter advised that attackers gained access to a subset of its data. A corpus of data was subsequently published publicly and contained 275k unique email addresses and Discord usernames.
A small number of records belonging to paying subscribers whose purchases were processed via Stripe were also present and included names, countries and postcodes.
how: In October 2026, the Discord server protection service Double Counter suffered a data breach attributed to a vulnerability in the Metabase analytics tool .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 274,922 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Geographic locations, Names, Usernames.
editorial: Double Counter's own site describes it as a Discord bot that blocks alternate accounts by comparing device, browser and network data, so the data it holds is, by design, the data that links accounts together.

That is what makes a leak of an anti-alt service different from an ordinary one: the pairing of an email address with a Discord username is exactly what someone running an alternate or anonymous account would least want published. The reported cause is also worth noticing. The breach was attributed to a vulnerability in Metabase, an analytics dashboard.

Internal tools like this are often left reachable from the internet with more access to raw data than any public page, and they tend to be patched last because nobody thinks of them as part of the product.

For most people in this set the practical risk is targeted phishing on Discord itself: messages that use your real username and mention the server-verification bot you remember using. Discord staff and verification bots do not ask for your password or a login code.
The small number of paying subscribers whose names, countries and postcodes were included carry more risk than the rest, because those details connect a gaming identity to a real person.

For moderators of servers that used the bot, the useful step is to post a short pinned message saying that no one from the server or the bot will ask for login codes, which removes the most common pretext before it is tried. Server owners should also think about what the bot was told.

Anti-alt services work by comparing signals between accounts, and if a moderator ever checked a suspected alt by hand, notes about that decision may live in the server's own logs rather than the bot's.

Reviewing what your moderation tools keep, and for how long, is the same lesson as with any third-party integration: the data you hand over is only as safe as the least-maintained dashboard that can read it.

background: In September 2026, the German political party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) suffered a data breach which exposed 345k unique email addresses. The following month, hundreds of gigabytes of data containing hundreds of thousands of emails and attachments was published online, with searchable AI-generated summaries and downloadable original files.

An analysis of the incident reported that the breach was detected as early as 9 September, with a subsequent intrusion occurring five days later. In its public statement , AfD attributed the breach to an attack on a hosting provider, identified in subsequent reporting as the party-owned Alternita Dienstleistungs GmbH.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 345,439 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Email messages.
editorial: Two data classes, but one of them is "email messages", and that is the part that matters. An email address list tells you who was on a mailing list. Hundreds of gigabytes of messages and attachments tell you what people wrote to a political party, which under European data protection law counts as special category data because it can reveal political opinions.
Have I Been Pwned flags this entry as sensitive. The publication format is new and worth watching. The data was released with searchable, AI-generated summaries alongside the original files.

That lowers the effort needed to find a named person in a leak from days of reading to a single search, which makes the exposure for anyone who merely wrote in, including people who are not members, far greater than the headline count of addresses suggests. The party attributed the breach to an attack on its hosting provider.

Whatever one thinks of the organisation, the lesson is general: correspondence sent to any campaign, charity or advocacy group sits on someone else's servers indefinitely. If you are in this set, assume messages you sent could be quoted back to you, and treat any contact that references them with caution.

HIBP marks this record as sensitive, which means it is not publicly searchable in the usual way: an address can only be checked by its verified owner. That design decision exists for exactly this kind of data, where simply being in the file says something about a person's political contact.

It is also why this archive page avoids any detail about individual correspondents and limits itself to what the record says about the incident. The timeline in the record, detection on 9 September and a second intrusion five days later, describes a problem that recurs across this archive: an organisation that discovers an intrusion does not always succeed in removing the intruder before they return.

For anyone who handles constituent or member correspondence, the lesson is to keep less of it for less time. Mail that has been deleted under a retention policy cannot be published, summarised or searched by anyone.

editorial: The distinction in this record is between professional contact information and an assumption about medical records. Have I Been Pwned's description says the addresses belonged predominantly to healthcare professionals, staff and leads. Its listed fields include employers, job titles and support tickets.

That does not establish that patient histories or clinical records were exposed, and this entry should not be read as making that additional claim. Support-ticket context can make a fraudulent follow-up more convincing than a generic message. A sender may mention a product, workplace or earlier enquiry and ask the recipient to open an attachment or change payment instructions.

This is a plausible risk from the listed fields, not evidence that such a campaign has been observed in this incident. Verify an unexpected request using a contact route you already know rather than the number or link inside the message.

For an organization, the useful response is to identify which business addresses and support interactions are affected, inform the appropriate internal security contact, and preserve suspicious messages through the normal reporting process. Do not circulate the leaked dataset to colleagues to look for their names.

A breach entry does not establish that your current account is compromised or that the affected service has reset its access controls. The source describes an extortion campaign and publication of allegedly obtained data. It does not document the exact intrusion path.

Keep that unknown separate from the published contact-data description; guessing an unpatched system or stolen credential would add a causal story the available record does not support. The record says the addresses belong predominantly to healthcare professionals, Medela staff and leads, and the field list includes salutations, employers and job titles.

For a medical device company, that profile is likely to include clinicians, clinic purchasers and distributors, people who receive product updates, training invitations and order confirmations as a normal part of their work. Those are the message types most worth checking twice. HIBP flags this entry as sensitive, which means it is only shown to someone who verifies ownership of an address.

If you are responsible for a clinic or a purchasing team and want to know whether staff are included, the domain search for your organisation's email domain is the route that respects that restriction, and it avoids circulating copies of the dataset internally.

The data consisted largely of corporate contact records and included 436k unique email addresses from mailing lists, employee records and other contacts.

editorial: This is one of a run of entries in the archive with the same shape: a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" demand, followed by publication of what is mostly corporate contact data. Neogen's set is mailing lists, employee records and business contacts, so most people in it are not customers in the consumer sense.

They are buyers, suppliers, lab staff and people who once filled in a form. Contact records sound harmless until you look at what they combine: name, salutation, employer, job title, direct phone number and work address. That is the exact kit needed for a convincing business email compromise.

An invoice that appears to come from a real supplier, addressed to the right person by title, and followed up by a phone call to their actual desk number is far more persuasive than a generic phishing email. If your work address is in this set, the people to warn are colleagues in accounts payable.

Any request to change a supplier's bank details, especially one that arrives with urgency, should be confirmed by calling a number you already had on file, not one in the message. Neogen works in food safety and animal health, so the business contacts in this file sit in supply chains that run on trust and paperwork: laboratories, farms, food manufacturers and distributors.

A fake certificate request, a fake test-kit order or a fake change to a recall notice would reach people who handle exactly those documents every week, and the leaked job titles make it easy to send each message to the right desk. Salutations appear in the field list too, which is a small but telling detail.

A message that addresses someone as "Dr." or by their correct title reads as if it came from someone who knows them, and formality is one of the cues people use to judge whether an email is genuine. Teams in this file can blunt that by agreeing that urgent document or payment requests, however correctly addressed, are confirmed by phone before anyone acts on them.

background: In August 2026, healthcare and pharmaceutical company McKesson was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign . The group subsequently published a substantial corpus of data they alleged was sourced from the company, which included 6.4M unique email addresses among other personal and corporate data attributes.
The impacted data related to a range of individuals and roles, including marketing campaign recipients, patients, staff and healthcare provider contacts.

In McKesson's disclosure notice , the company advised it had identified unauthorised access to "certain third-party applications and the exfiltration of certain data was associated with a subset of customers within our Oncology & Multispecialty and Medical-Surgical business units", but had "reasonable assurance of no ongoing unauthorized activity".

motive: In August 2026, healthcare and pharmaceutical company McKesson was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 6,404,340 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Employers, Genders, Names, Personal health data, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Read the data classes rather than the headline. "Personal health data" sitting next to names, dates of birth, employers and addresses is the combination that makes a breach at a distributor behave like a breach at a hospital, and McKesson is a wholesaler, not a care provider. Most of the people in this file have never knowingly had a relationship with it.

That is the pattern worth internalising about healthcare supply chains. The companies holding your health data are rarely the ones you chose: they are the clearing houses, distributors, benefit administrators and billing intermediaries that sit behind the clinic. You cannot audit them, opt out of them, or in most cases name them. The practical consequence is narrow and specific.

Health-adjacent detail is what makes a fraudulent call convincing, a caller who knows your employer, your date of birth and something about your medication has not proved they are your pharmacy. Treat any unexpected contact referencing your care as unverified, and go back through a number you already had. HIBP lists four groups inside the data: marketing campaign recipients, patients, staff and healthcare provider contacts.

That mix means two very different fraud risks run in parallel. Patients face health-themed social engineering, such as fake prescription refill calls, fake insurance reviews and fake billing disputes. Provider contacts and staff face business fraud, such as fake purchase orders, fake account changes for supplier payments and requests to "re-verify" access to ordering portals.

The company's notice refers to unauthorised access to certain third-party applications. For a clinic or pharmacy that orders through a distributor, the practical step is to agree a call-back procedure for any change to delivery addresses, bank details or ordering credentials, so that a convincing email carrying real names and account context is not enough on its own to move money or medicine.

editorial: The published corpus contained millions of synthetic records, fabricated rows matching no real person, which were identified and excluded before the figure of 12.9 million was settled on.

That detail is worth more than the breach itself, because the number an extortion crew posts and the number of people actually in the file are routinely different numbers, and the first one is the one that becomes the headline. Padding pays twice.

A larger file sells for more, and a company forced to answer for an inflated figure looks worse than it is, which is useful leverage when the demand is "pay or we publish". What genuinely leaked here is ordinary: name, email address, phone number, home address. No passwords, no card numbers, nothing that opens an account. That combination does not get into anything, it gets a convincing message about a delivery problem on an order you could plausibly have placed.

The uptick in parcel texts after a retail breach is not a coincidence, and it is the whole return on data like this. Workwear is also bought by trades and businesses, and a physical address in a retail file may be a job site or a company yard rather than a home.

For small businesses that order equipment and clothing for staff, the leaked address and phone number are enough for a convincing fake invoice or a "bulk order confirmation" that asks for payment to a new account. The safe habit is the same as for consumers: pay only through accounts and portals you set up yourself.

The group subsequently published data it claimed was taken from Sharecare's systems, containing 318k unique email addresses. Most of the data consisted of B2B sales and marketing records with names, physical addresses, phone numbers, job titles and employers.
The data also included a small number of Brazilian health insurance plan members, including dates of birth, genders, marital statuses and CPF numbers (Brazilian taxpayer identification numbers).

motive: In August 2026, the digital health company Sharecare was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 318,185 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

editorial: Most of this data is B2B sales and marketing records, the same kind of business contact list that appears in several other ShinyHunters releases. Read only the headline and you would file it as a nuisance.
The detail that changes that is in the last line of the record: a small number of Brazilian health plan members, with dates of birth, genders, marital statuses and CPF numbers.

A CPF is Brazil's taxpayer identification number, and it is used far more widely than its name suggests: opening bank accounts, signing up for phone contracts, buying online, and proving identity to almost any service. Paired with a name and date of birth it is enough to attempt credit and account fraud in that person's name.

A small number of records can carry more real harm than hundreds of thousands of work email addresses. That is a pattern worth recognising in breach reporting generally. The size of a set and its severity are different measurements. If you hold a Brazilian plan connected to Sharecare, monitoring your CPF for new credit activity matters more here than changing any password.

The B2B majority of the file has its own, more ordinary risk. For a digital health company, sales and marketing records are likely to describe the people who buy health services on behalf of others, such as benefits managers, HR leads and plan administrators.

Those are the people who receive genuine messages about enrolment periods and programme renewals, which makes them a natural audience for a fake renewal invoice or a fake "update your plan portal login" email. The record also shows how far a single incident can travel across borders.

A United States digital health company, a criminal group publishing worldwide, and a small group of Brazilian plan members whose CPF numbers ended up in the same release. Data protection law in Brazil (the LGPD) and in the United States treats those records very differently, but the people in them face the same practical question: whether anyone has used their details to open something new.
For the Brazilian members, checking for credit or accounts opened in your CPF is the step that answers it.

background: In August 2026, data centre operator CyrusOne was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt . The group subsequently published data allegedly obtained from the company, which included 373k unique email addresses across records relating to users, sales leads and CyrusOne employees. The data largely consisted of corporate contact information, including names, physical addresses, phone numbers and job titles.
It also included support tickets and other information related to the organisation's operations.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In August 2026, data centre operator CyrusOne was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt .

The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Support tickets.
editorial: A data centre operator's contact list is a map of who runs other companies' infrastructure. The people in this set are not random consumers: they are users of the platform, sales leads and CyrusOne employees, which means facilities managers, network engineers and the people who can authorise physical or remote access to servers.

The field that makes this more than a contact list is support tickets. Tickets at a data centre are where customers describe access requests, hardware changes and outages in their own words, sometimes naming the systems involved. Like any support record, they also capture whatever someone typed while trying to get a problem fixed quickly.

The realistic follow-on attack is social engineering aimed at the help desk, from either direction: someone posing as a customer to request access, or posing as CyrusOne staff to ask a customer to "confirm" credentials.

If you manage infrastructure hosted there, treat any unexpected access or credential request as suspect until it is verified through a channel you set up before this leak, and check whether your old tickets mention anything that should be rotated.

The extortion pattern in the record, a "pay or leak" demand followed by publication, is shared by a run of entries in this archive attributed to the same group, including McKesson , Crunchbase and Harvard . Read together, those records show the target was rarely consumer passwords. It was business relationship data: who works where, who buys what, and who to call.

CyrusOne fits that shape exactly. Physical addresses carry a particular weight for a data centre operator. Facility locations are often kept low-profile for security reasons, and a file that ties named engineers and customer contacts to sites and phone numbers gives anyone planning a pretext visit or a tailgating attempt a cast list.
Operators and tenants in this file should brief reception and security staff that a visitor who knows the right names is not, on that basis alone, expected or authorised.

background: In August 2026, millions of records allegedly sourced from Chess.com were posted online . The data contained 7.3M rows with 4.6M unique email addresses, along with usernames, names, countries and data relating to users' Chess.com accounts. Analysis of the data suggested it had been obtained by scraping.
When loaded into HIBP, 99% of the email addresses had already appeared in previous data breaches, further supporting the scraping theory. Read more about scrapes and data breaches.
how: Analysis of the data suggested it had been obtained by scraping.
When loaded into HIBP, 99% of the email addresses had already appeared in previous data breaches, further supporting the scraping theory.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 4,653,212 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Geographic locations, Names, Usernames.
editorial: Two details in this record deserve more weight than the total. The first is that analysis indicated the data was scraped rather than taken from a database, collected through interfaces that were working as designed, at a scale nobody intended. The second is that 99% of the addresses had already appeared in earlier breaches.

Both facts cut the same way, and not in the direction most people assume. A scrape means no password was exposed, so there is nothing to reset. A 99% overlap with previous incidents means almost nobody in this file is newly exposed.

If you are in it, this is very unlikely to be the breach that matters to you, one of the earlier ones already was. What it does add is linkage. A username joined to a real name, a country and a confirmed email address is exactly the material used to connect a pseudonymous account to a person.

If your chess handle is one you also use elsewhere, that connection is now easier for anyone to make, and no password change undoes it. The record counts 7.3 million rows but 4.6 million unique email addresses, which says something about how the data was collected.

A scrape that returns several rows per person, or records for the same account seen more than once, inflates the raw total. The unique count is the better measure, and even that includes accounts that may no longer be active. Online games with rating systems and public profiles are also a place where children and adults mix.

A username, a real name and a country are exactly the fields a parent would least want connected for a young player. If a child in your household plays online chess, this is a good moment to check that their profile shows a display name rather than their full name, and that the email on the account is one an adult manages.

background: In May 2026, the French holiday rental network Gîtes de France suffered a data breach affecting some of its departmental branches. editorial: Gîtes de France operates through departmental branches, and the breach affected some of them rather than the whole network. A branch structure is common for federations, franchises and cooperatives, and it tends to mean many separate systems with uneven security, any one of which can expose customers who only ever dealt with the national brand. The data class that sets this apart is booking details.
A holiday booking says where someone will be and, by implication, when their home will be empty.

Combined with a postal address, that is information a burglar would value, though for most people the more likely misuse is fraud: a message about "your upcoming stay" that knows the property, the dates and the guest's name, asking for a deposit to be paid again or a card to be re-confirmed. Holiday rental scams already rely on urgency and plausibility.

A leak that supplies the real booking removes the main thing that used to give them away. If you booked through a Gîtes de France branch, confirm any payment request directly with the owner or branch using contact details from your original confirmation, never from the message asking for money. The record dates the breach to May 2026, with the data reaching HIBP in October.

For a holiday rental network, that timing matters: a summer of real bookings fell between the two dates, so the booking details in the file may describe stays that have now happened as well as stays still to come.

Past stays still have value to a fraudster as proof of a relationship, such as a refund for a disputed cleaning fee or a satisfaction survey with a prize. Property owners who rent through the network are worth a thought as well.

Booking records connect owners' properties with guests' names and dates, and a fraudster can work either side: telling a guest the owner needs payment to a new account, or telling an owner that a guest's payment failed and needs to be resent.
Owners who notice guests receiving odd payment requests should tell their branch, because a pattern of complaints is often how a branch discovers its booking data is being used.

background: In April 2026, education company McGraw Hill confirmed a data breach following an extortion attempt . Attributed to a Salesforce misconfiguration, the company stated the incident exposed "a limited set of data from a webpage hosted by Salesforce on its platform".

More than 100GB of data was later publicly distributed, containing 13.5M unique email addresses across multiple files, with additional fields such as name, physical address and phone number appearing inconsistently across some records.
how: Attributed to a Salesforce misconfiguration, the company stated the incident exposed "a limited set of data from a webpage hosted by Salesforce on its platform".
motive: In April 2026, education company McGraw Hill confirmed a data breach following an extortion attempt .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 13,500,136 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

editorial: Read the disclosure language and the outcome side by side. The company described "a limited set of data from a webpage hosted by Salesforce on its platform". More than 100GB was subsequently published, carrying 13.5 million distinct email addresses.

Both statements can be technically accurate at the same time, one describes the surface that was exposed, the other describes what came through it, and that is exactly why a description of the entry point is not a measure of the damage. The other thing worth noticing is whose data this is.

Students and instructors did not choose McGraw Hill; an institution chose it for them, and the record that ended up in a 100GB archive was created as a condition of taking a course. That pattern runs through most education technology breaches, and it is why "stop using the service" is advice that does not apply here.

Physical addresses and phone numbers appear only in some of the records here, which HIBP describes as appearing inconsistently across files. That matters for anyone checking whether they are affected. Finding your email in the data does not tell you how much else was attached to it, and not finding your postal address in one copy does not mean it was absent from another.
When the source is a set of distributed files rather than one database export, the honest assumption is the fuller one. The audience shapes the scams.

Education publishers hold accounts for students, instructors and school administrators, and the messages that follow look like course access problems, expiring textbook licences, refunds for digital materials, or an instructor asking students to log in somewhere new before an assignment is due.
Students are a particularly exposed group, because they are used to being sent to unfamiliar login pages by their courses and many are handling their first accounts of this kind.

If you teach, this is worth a sentence to your class: course platforms do not ask for passwords or payment details by email, and any change to where students log in will come through the institution's own systems.

If you are a student in the file, the most useful step is to check whether the email address on your McGraw Hill account is your school address or a personal one, because that decides which inbox the follow-up phishing will land in.

editorial: Fourteen categories of data in one record, including bank account numbers, passwords and financial transactions, is close to the worst combination a single breach can produce. It is also an unsurprising one for a gig-economy platform: paying people requires banking details, verifying them requires identity data, and running the marketplace generates a behavioural record on top.

The four-month gap in this record is the part to sit with. Data was claimed and listed for sale in March; it was published in July. For anyone in the file, exposure began at the earlier date, every warning, every reset, every "we are investigating" statement in the interim was issued about data that was already in someone else's hands.

The order of response matters here more than usual. Bank details cannot be changed as easily as a password, so start by watching the account rather than trying to fix it: unexpected small transactions are the standard test before a larger one. Then kill the password everywhere it was reused.

People who earn through platforms like this are also disproportionately targeted by "your payout failed" messages, which work because they arrive at a moment the recipient is genuinely expecting money. Profile photos and device information appear in the field list alongside the financial data, and together they make this one of the more complete identity records in the archive.

A face, a name, a date of birth and a bank account number are the components of a convincing fake identity for opening accounts elsewhere, especially on platforms that verify users by comparing a selfie with a document. Workers in this file should watch for verification emails from services they never joined.

Personal interests and education levels are the kind of fields a platform collects to match workers with tasks. In a breach they become the hooks for fake job offers: a survey panel, a remote task or a "premium earning tier" that fits what the person said they liked.
Those offers often ask for a small activation fee or for bank details to "set up payouts", and the second request should be the alarm, because a genuine platform already has them.

editorial: Credit scores, income levels, government-issued IDs and latitude and longitude pairs, in the same file. Each is serious on its own; together they describe a person's financial position and physical location precisely enough to select targets from the data itself. That is the specific risk with lending platforms, and it is different from the risk at a retailer. A shop knows what you bought.

A lender knows what you can afford, what you owe, how you were assessed and where you were when you applied. Fraud built on that is not scattergun, it is addressed to the people the file identifies as most likely to accept an offer of credit, using the detail that makes the offer look like it came from someone who already holds their business.

The government ID numbers are the part with no expiry date. A password is a weekend of work to replace; a national identity document number is not replaceable on request in most countries, and it will still be valid years from now.

Where your jurisdiction offers a credit freeze or credit ban, this is the record that justifies using it, it blocks the specific fraud this combination of fields enables. The record describes where the email addresses came from: credit scoring requests, credit bureau records, customer identity records and email validation logs. Those sources mean the file is not only people who bought something with Addi.

Credit scoring requests and bureau records can include people who were assessed and declined, or who started an application and stopped. If you think you never used the service, you may still appear because a shop you visited ran a check. Latitude and longitude pairs are rare in a breach and especially sensitive wherever phone extortion is a known risk.

A location point tied to a name and an estimated income is a short list for that kind of call. Anyone in the file who receives a threatening or high-pressure call that cites their address or finances should end it and report it to the police, rather than negotiating or confirming any detail.

motive: In February 2026, the automotive marketplace CarGurus was the target of a data breach attributed to the threat actor ShinyHunters .

Following an attempted extortion, the data was published publicly and contained more than 12M email addresses across multiple files including user account ID mappings, finance pre-qualification application data and dealer account and subscription information.

editorial: One phrase in the field list deserves a stop: finance pre-qualification application data. Those are people who asked a car marketplace what they could borrow, a question nobody asks idly, and the answer is sitting beside their name, phone number and home address. Intent is the part of a breach that rarely makes the summary and reliably makes the fraud.

Knowing that someone is shopping for a car, and roughly what they can finance, tells a caller which pretext will land: a rate they have been approved for, a deposit to hold a vehicle, a dealer following up on the application they really did fill in last week. Generic scams get hung up on. This one continues a conversation the victim started.

Dealer account and subscription records were in the same release, which hands the same caller both ends of that conversation, the buyer's details and a real dealership to impersonate. The defence is procedural rather than technical: anything about a vehicle purchase, a finance offer or a deposit gets confirmed by ringing the dealer on a number you looked up yourself.
Never the number in the message, however well the message knows you. The record also mentions user account ID mappings, a technical detail with a practical consequence.

Mapping tables link one identifier to another, such as a marketplace account to a finance application or a dealer subscription, and they are what allows the separate files in a release like this to be joined into fuller profiles. A leak of contact data alone is a list. A leak that includes the joins is closer to a database.

background: In January 2026, the private company intelligence platform Crunchbase was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt . Data allegedly obtained from the company was subsequently published publicly and included 560k unique email addresses, largely belonging to leads and business contacts. Other data included names, physical addresses, phone numbers, job titles, employers and LinkedIn profiles.
Crunchbase later confirmed that a threat actor had exfiltrated documents from its corporate network.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In January 2026, the private company intelligence platform Crunchbase was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 559,908 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Social media profiles.
editorial: There is an irony in a company-intelligence platform losing its own contact data. Crunchbase is in the business of organising information about businesses and the people in them, and what leaked was largely its leads and business contacts: names, employers, job titles, phone numbers, addresses and LinkedIn profiles. The LinkedIn field is what makes this set unusually ready to use.

Most leaked contact lists need some work before an attacker can be sure the person and the job are current. A profile link does that work: it confirms the role, shows the reporting line and supplies the photo and history needed to impersonate a colleague or a recruiter convincingly.

Crunchbase later confirmed that documents were exfiltrated from its corporate network, so this is not only a scraped list. Founders, investors and executives are over-represented in a dataset like this, and they are the usual targets for fake investment offers, fake board introductions and invoice fraud.

If you are in it, be sceptical of unsolicited deal flow that seems to know exactly who you are and who you work with. The date gap is also unusually long for a 2026 incident. The extortion attempt took place in January, and the data reached HIBP in October.

For nine months a curated list of business contacts with their roles and LinkedIn profiles was available to whoever had it, and the people in it are precisely the ones who receive cold outreach every day, which makes a targeted approach hard to tell from normal business traffic. For companies whose staff appear in the file, the most effective response is procedural rather than individual.

Agree internally that changes to payment details, wire instructions or investment terms are confirmed by a call to a known number, and make it normal for staff to ask for that confirmation even when a request appears to come from a founder or an investor they know. The leaked fields make impersonation easy.
A rule like that makes it slow, and slow is usually enough to stop it.

background: In December 2025, SoundCloud announced it had discovered unauthorised activity on its platform . The incident allowed an attacker to map publicly available SoundCloud profile data to email addresses for approximately 20% of its users. The impacted data included 30M unique email addresses, names, usernames, avatars, follower and following counts and, in some cases, the user’s country.
The attackers later attempted to extort SoundCloud before publicly releasing the data the following month.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: The attackers later attempted to extort SoundCloud before publicly releasing the data the following month.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 29,815,722 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Avatars, Email addresses, Geographic locations, Names, Profile statistics, Usernames.
editorial: Nothing in this breach was secret. Display names, avatars, follower counts and countries were all public on the platform, and the email addresses were not. The attacker's entire contribution was joining the two, for roughly a fifth of the user base. That join is the product.
A handle chosen precisely because it is not your name is worth very little on its own; attached to a mailbox you actually read, it becomes an identity and a delivery channel at the same time.

Artists who released work under an alias and listeners whose taste they would rather not have attributed to them are in the same file, and no amount of care about what they posted would have kept them out of it, the private half came from the account system, not from anything they published. The practical exposure is phishing with an unusually good hook.

A message quoting your real handle, your follower count and your country reads exactly like the platform, and the platform is precisely who a working musician expects to hear from about payouts, copyright claims and takedowns. Open the app and look; do not follow the link, however specific the message is about a track you genuinely uploaded.

The record says the mapping covered about 20 percent of users, and that is worth checking before assuming you are affected. Not finding your address does not prove your profile was outside the mapped set, because coverage of any breach search depends on the data the service received.

Finding it means the link between your handle and that address is now public, and it will remain so even if you change the email on the account later. The extortion sequence in the record is also familiar: the platform discovered unauthorised activity in December 2025, the attackers attempted to extort SoundCloud, and the data was released publicly the following month.

For creators, the practical step is to separate the address used for the account from any address used for bookings or label contacts, so that a phishing message sent to the leaked address is easier to recognise as such.

background: In November 2025, AI music generation tool Suno suffered a data breach that later came to light in July the following year . The data contained over 55M unique email addresses. Phone numbers were also present where they had been used as the sign-up method.

Although representing a small portion of the corpus, the breach also included tens of thousands of Stripe records relating to purchases, containing names, physical addresses, purchase amounts and partial credit card data including the card type, expiry date and last 4 digits. The company advised that "Suno does not have access to customers' full credit card numbers in Stripe".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 55,282,226 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Partial credit card data, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Purchases.
editorial: Eight months passed between the breach date on this record and the point at which it came to light. That gap is the most useful thing on the page.

Everyone in the file spent most of a year with no reason to change anything, while the data was already out, which is why "there is no evidence of misuse" is a statement about what the company can see, not about what has happened. The second detail worth noticing is the shape of the exposure.

Fifty-five million email addresses with names and phone numbers is a contact list. The tens of thousands of payment records inside it are a different category entirely: a much smaller group, exposed far more seriously, buried inside a number so large that the distinction disappears from most coverage.

If you only ever generated a few tracks and never paid, your realistic risk is targeted phishing that references a service you actually used. If you bought anything, you are in the smaller set, check the card statement for that period specifically, and treat any message about a subscription or refund as unverified until you have opened the account yourself.

The record notes that phone numbers appear where they were used as the sign-up method. That is a detail many people will not remember choosing, and it means someone who signed up with a phone number to try an AI music tool may now find that number linked to their name and email in a public file.

Phone numbers are the identifier used for SMS sign-in codes and account recovery on many other services, which makes them more valuable to an attacker than they look. For paying customers, the company's statement that it does not have access to full card numbers held by Stripe is consistent with the field list, which shows only card type, expiry and last four digits.

Those are not enough to make a purchase, but they are enough to sound like the payment provider. A message that quotes those details and asks you to "re-verify" a card for a subscription renewal is the scam this data enables. Manage the subscription from inside the app or the website you log into yourself.

background: In November 2025, Harvard University suffered a data breach later linked to a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt . The data contained 851k unique email addresses relating to the university's alumni and fundraising systems, along with extensive profile information for donors, alumni, parents and some faculty, staff and students.

In Harvard's disclosure notice , the university stated that the breach impacted "personal information such as email addresses, telephone numbers, home and business addresses, event attendance, details of donations to the University, and other biographical information pertaining to University fundraising and alumni engagement activities".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In November 2025, Harvard University suffered a data breach later linked to a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 850,537 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

The reported exposed data includes Charitable donations, Citizenship statuses, Dates of birth, Education levels, Email addresses, Employers, Ethnicities, Family members' names, Genders, Job titles, Marital statuses, Names, Occupations, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Places of birth, Salutations, Social media profiles.
editorial: Eighteen data classes is a lot, and the list reads like the fields of a fundraising database, because that is what it came from: alumni engagement and donor records. Charitable donations, family members' names, ethnicities, places of birth, citizenship statuses and marital statuses are not things a university needs to teach anyone.

They are things a development office collects to decide whom to ask for money, and how much. That is the uncomfortable point about this breach. The most detailed profiles belong to the people with the closest relationship to the institution: donors, alumni and parents.

Donation history in particular is a ready-made target list, because it says who gives, how much and to what, which is exactly what a fake charity appeal or a fake "alumni office" call needs. Harvard's notice describes the data as relating to fundraising and alumni engagement.

If you are a Harvard alum or donor, expect approaches that cite real gifts, real classmates or real family members. A genuine development office will never object to you hanging up and calling the number on the university's own website.
The field list also includes citizenship statuses and places of birth, which are unusual in any breach and sensitive in a particular way for international students and alumni.

Fraud aimed at people with visa or immigration concerns often impersonates officials and uses fear rather than greed, and a caller who knows where someone was born, what they studied and where they now work can sound very official indeed. Anyone in that position should know that immigration authorities do not demand payment over the phone or by gift card.

The year between the November 2025 breach and the November 2026 HIBP date also matters: donation records, event attendance and family details may have been used for targeting before most alumni could check whether they were included.

Universities send many genuine fundraising messages, so a useful habit is to make any donation through the giving page you reach yourself, not through a link or phone number supplied by a caller or an email, however much it seems to know.

editorial: The size is not the interesting part. What matters here is the two-month gap: the ransomware group claimed the intrusion in November, and the data only reached a public forum in January. For anyone in that file, the exposure began long before there was anything to read about it.

That gap is the norm rather than the exception, which is why "we have seen no evidence of misuse" in a disclosure statement means considerably less than it sounds like. Look at which fields sit together in this file: date of birth, gender, a geographic location and purchase information, attached to a name and an email address. That is not a login record.

It is a customer profile of the kind a retailer builds for marketing, and it describes a person in more detail than most account dumps do. Someone holding it knows roughly where you live, how old you are, and what you bought from a sportswear brand, which is enough to write a message that sounds exactly like the company.

The fraud that follows a retail file like this one is rarely clever. It is an order confirmation you did not place, a delivery that needs a small redelivery fee, a refund for a product you really did buy, or a loyalty reward that expires today. Each of those works better when the sender can quote a real purchase.

If you shopped with Under Armour, the defence is to stop treating a correct order detail as proof that a message is genuine, and to check orders by typing the retailer's address yourself rather than following a link. The record also lists no passwords, and that is worth saying plainly because it changes what helps.

Resetting your Under Armour password is harmless but does not touch the problem. The exposure here is personal detail that cannot be changed, so the response is attention over time: a date of birth paired with your name and location is a standard verification question, and it is worth asking your bank or phone carrier whether they still accept it on its own.

background: In October 2025, retailer Canadian Tire was the victim of a data breach that exposed almost 42M records. The data contained 38M unique email addresses along with names, phone numbers and physical addresses. Passwords were stored as PBKDF2 hashes and for a subset of records, dates of birth and partial credit card data were also included (card type, expiry and masked card number).
In its disclosure notice , Canadian Tire advised that the incident did not impact bank account information or loyalty program data.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 38,306,562 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Genders, Names, Partial credit card data, Passwords, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: The passwords in this one were stored as PBKDF2 hashes, which is the thing most companies in this archive got wrong and Canadian Tire got right. It is worth saying plainly, because breach coverage rarely does: a strong, slow hash means the password field is the part of this file least likely to hurt you. The part that will is the combination underneath it.

Name, date of birth, address, phone number and the card type, expiry and last four digits, all in one row. The disclosure notes that bank account information was not affected, which is true and beside the point, nobody defrauds a retail customer by knowing their account number.

They do it by calling with the last four digits of the card, the correct expiry, and the customer's own date of birth, which is a script this file writes for them. Masked card data is classified as low sensitivity because it cannot be used to transact. It can be used to be believed, and that is the attack that follows a retail breach.
The record also gives the size of the gap between breach and visibility. The breach date is October 2025, and the data reached HIBP in February 2026.

That is a gap of roughly four months, and the first useful question for anyone in the file is not whether they were affected but which details were attached to their row: the date of birth and partial card data appear only for a subset.

The company states that loyalty programme data was not affected, which matters because loyalty accounts are where points can be spent quickly by someone else. That leaves the familiar retail scripts: delivery problems, warranty claims on large purchases such as tyres or appliances, and refund offers that ask you to "confirm" the card you used.
If a caller can quote the card type, expiry and last four digits, that is evidence they have this file, not evidence they work for the retailer.

Prosper advised that they did not find any evidence of unauthorised access to customer accounts and funds, and that their customer-facing operations were uninterrupted. Further information about the incident is contained in Prosper's FAQs .
how: In September 2025, Prosper announced that it had detected unauthorised access to their systems, which resulted in the exposure of customer and applicant information .
Prosper advised that they did not find any evidence of unauthorised access to customer accounts and funds, and that their customer-facing operations were uninterrupted.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 17,605,276 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

The reported exposed data includes Browser user agent details, Credit status information, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Employment statuses, Government issued IDs, Income levels, IP addresses, Names, Physical addresses.
editorial: Read the accompanying statement carefully: no evidence of unauthorised access to customer accounts. That can be entirely true at the same moment that 17.6 million people's Social Security numbers, incomes, employment status and credit standing have left the building. Account access and data theft are two different claims, and only one of them was being answered.

A lending platform holds the most complete financial identity most people ever assemble in one place, and it holds it for applicants as well as customers. People who were declined, or who filled in the form and thought better of it, have no account, no login, no dashboard and no particular reason to have been watching for a notice.

They are in the file all the same. This is one of the few entries in this archive where the usual advice is insufficient. A government identifier cannot be reissued because it leaked, so the only durable control is limiting what can be opened in your name.

A credit freeze at each bureau is free, takes a few minutes, and lifts again when you actually need credit. It is the specific countermeasure for the specific data that left here, and it works whether or not anyone ever touches your Prosper account. The field list includes browser user agent details and IP addresses, which are the traces left by applying online.

They are less sensitive than the financial fields, but they show that the data includes the technical record of the application session as well as the answers, which is useful to fraudsters trying to imitate a known user's device when applying for credit elsewhere.

The record also points to Prosper's own FAQs about the incident, which is the right place for anyone in the file to check what protections the company is offering and for how long. Monitoring offered after a breach usually covers a fixed period, while an exposed SSN stays usable much longer, so a freeze remains the longer-lasting step even if you accept the monitoring offer.

background: During 2025, the threat-intelligence firm Synthient aggregated 2 billion unique email addresses disclosed in credential-stuffing lists found across multiple malicious internet sources . Comprised of email addresses and passwords from previous data breaches, these lists are used by attackers to compromise other, unrelated accounts of victims who have reused their passwords.

The data also included 1.3 billion unique passwords, which are now searchable in Pwned Passwords. Working to turn breached data into awareness, Synthient partnered with HIBP to help victims of cybercrime understand their exposure.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 1,957,476,021 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: This entry is not a company being breached. It is an aggregate, two billion addresses collected from credential-stuffing lists that were already circulating, built from other people's breaches and from information-stealing malware on victims' own machines. Nobody was attacked to create it. Which means finding yourself here answers a different question than usual. It does not tell you which service failed.

It tells you that a password of yours, from somewhere, at some point, is in the pool that gets tried automatically against banks, mailboxes and retailers. That is worse in one specific way: there is no single site to go and fix. The part people miss is the stealer-log component.

Credentials harvested by malware come from a compromised device, not a compromised website, so they can include passwords that were never leaked by any company, typed into sites that have never been breached at all. If that is the source, changing one password is not enough; the machine that captured it needs to be cleaned first, or the replacement joins the same list.

The useful response is boringly structural. Unique passwords everywhere, generated and stored in a manager, and two-factor authentication on anything that can reset something else. Aggregates like this one are the reason credential stuffing works at all, and they are the reason it stops working against people who never reuse. The scale needs one clarification.

Two billion unique email addresses is far more than the number of active internet users with a single address each, which reflects how many old, duplicate, disposable and machine-generated addresses accumulate in these lists.

The figure measures the size of the pool attackers draw from rather than the number of people affected, and the right question for an individual is not how big the list is but whether a password they still use is in it. The 1.3 billion passwords added to Pwned Passwords make that question answerable without exposing anything new.
The check uses a range query that sends only the first characters of a hash of the password, never the password itself, which is how the password tool on this site works as well.
If a password you use appears, the number next to it says how many times it was seen in breach data, and any count above zero is a reason to replace it.

background: During 2025, Synthient aggregated billions of records of "threat data" from various internet sources . The data contained 183M unique email addresses alongside the websites they were entered into and the passwords used. After normalising and deduplicating the data, 183 million unique email addresses remained, each linked to the website where the credentials were captured, and the password used.
This dataset is now searchable in HIBP by email address, password, domain, and the site on which the credentials were entered.
how: The records came from information-stealing malware on people's devices, rather than a single company database.
outcome: 182,962,095 email addresses are listed in the collection. This does not establish the number of people or service accounts affected.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: Synthient aggregated records from multiple sources during 2025. Have I Been Pwned describes a processing step that matters when reading the headline. After the data had been normalized and duplicates removed, approximately 183 million distinct email addresses remained. That number counts addresses across the collection. It gives no device count and no count of successful sign-ins.

The date HIBP added the collection, 21 October 2025, is a publication milestone. It cannot date an individual exposure. HIBP catalogue entry for Synthient Stealer Log Threat Data . Suppose you own a mailbox and use it at three online shops.

If that address appears against all three shops, it can contribute one to the distinct-address total while the website associations still identify three accounts worth checking. If two addresses forward to your inbox, both could contribute to the total even though you control them. These examples explain how the count works. The published summary gives no breakdown of how frequently either situation occurred.

The website associated with a record can help you decide what to check first. From a trusted device, go directly to a service you recognize and inspect its recent sessions, recovery details and sign-in notifications. Replace an exposed or reused password, revoke unfamiliar sessions and enable stronger sign-in protection where available.

For a work account, the account owner and the device administrator may have different pieces of evidence. Share the collection name and the time you received the alert without including any password. Readers comparing this entry with the ALIEN TXTBASE collection should keep the counts separate. Each publisher reports distinct addresses within its own dataset.

Calculating how many distinct addresses appeared across both would require knowing their overlap. Neither catalogue summary gives that figure. Adding the two headline counts would count any shared address twice.

background: In February 2025, 23 billion rows of stealer logs were obtained from a Telegram channel known as ALIEN TXTBASE . The data contained 284M unique email addresses alongside the websites they were entered into and the passwords used. This data is now searchable in HIBP by both email domain and the domain of the target website.
how: The records came from information-stealing malware on people's devices, rather than a single company database.
outcome: 284,132,969 email addresses are listed in the collection. This does not establish the number of people or service accounts affected.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: Two numbers describe ALIEN TXTBASE. Have I Been Pwned reports that the material obtained in February 2025 contained 23 billion rows. Across those rows, it identified 284,132,969 distinct email addresses. A row can repeat a previously seen address, including when the address appears against another website.

Dividing the row count by the address count would tell you nothing reliable about how many accounts an individual lost. HIBP catalogue entry for ALIEN TXTBASE . The name causes confusion in searches. HIBP files the collection under the ID AlienStealerLogs, while people write it as ALIEN TXTBASE, Alien Txtbase, AlienTxtBase or "alien text base". All of these refer to the same thing.

HIBP says the data came from "a Telegram channel known as ALIEN TXTBASE", and Troy Hunt's write-up describes the corpus as 744 files published to that channel as free samples, with newer logs sold by subscription. Troy Hunt on processing the ALIEN TXTBASE logs .

Searches for a download or for the channel itself usually come from people trying to find out whether their own details are inside. You do not need the files for that, and fetching them means handling other people's stolen passwords and opening files from a criminal channel.

Check your email address against HIBP or the MyRecon breach archive instead: the answer tells you whether you are listed and against which websites, without touching the raw logs. Consider a fictional record that pairs reader@example.org with shop.example. The email domain in this example is example.org. The website domain is shop.example.

Someone investigating the mailbox and someone responsible for the shop could therefore be looking at the same row for different reasons. Its presence says the two strings appeared together. Establishing when a particular device was infected, who operated it, or whether someone successfully signed in requires separate evidence such as device records and the shop's sign-in history.

There is a practical reason to keep those distinctions. After the initial publication, HIBP described additional work cleaning the domain associations and backfilling older collections. A count in a dated article and the domain associations returned by a later search can answer different questions.

When recording an exposure for your own accounts, note the name of the collection, the date you checked it and the service you recognize. Keep passwords and full log entries out of support requests. HIBP's March 2025 follow-up on data quality . If a listed service is yours, open it directly on a device you trust. Review active sessions and recent security events.

Replace an exposed password and any copies you reused, beginning with the mailbox used for account recovery. If you suspect a work device, give your security team the collection name and the time of the alert so they can check the endpoint and account records together.

breaches.title: 1win
breaches.summary: In November 2024, the online betting platform 1win suffered a data breach that exposed 96M users. The exposed data included email and IP addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, country and SHA-256 password hashes.

background: In November 2024, the online betting platform 1win suffered a data breach that exposed 96M users . The exposed data included email and IP addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, country and SHA-256 password hashes.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 96,166,543 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Geographic locations, IP addresses, Passwords, Phone numbers.
editorial: The password hashes in this breach were SHA-256, which sounds reassuring and is not. SHA-256 is a general-purpose hash built for speed, the same property that makes it excellent for verifying files makes it poor for storing passwords, because consumer graphics hardware can test enormous numbers of candidates per second. Proper password storage uses a deliberately slow algorithm with a per-user salt.

Anyone whose password appears in a wordlist should assume it has been recovered. The more sensitive issue is the context rather than the fields. A gambling account is inherently disclosive: its existence says something about a person that they may not have shared, and in several jurisdictions online betting is restricted or prohibited outright.

Dates of birth, phone numbers, IP addresses and country data attached to that account make the holder identifiable and locatable. That combination is what makes this data useful for extortion rather than ordinary fraud, the threat being exposure, not theft.

If a message arrives demanding payment to keep an account quiet, the data behind it has been public for a long time and payment buys nothing. Report it rather than engage. And change the password everywhere it was reused, starting with any account tied to money.

The record lists country among the exposed fields, and for a betting platform that is more than a demographic detail. It shows which users were placing bets from places where online gambling is restricted, and those users are the least likely to report an extortion attempt to the police, which is exactly why they are attractive targets.

The data being old does not change that calculation for the extortionist. Anyone in this file who is worried about their gambling, as distinct from the breach, should know that self-exclusion and blocking tools exist in many countries and on most phones and banking apps, and that a breach notice is a reasonable moment to use them.
For the account itself: close it if you no longer use it, so that the email and phone number on file stop being a live route for anyone with this data to try a password reset.

breaches.title: Hot Topic
breaches.summary: In October 2024, retailer Hot Topic suffered a data breach that exposed 57 million unique email addresses. The impacted data also included physical addresses, phone numbers, purchases, genders, dates of birth and partial credit data containing card type, expiry and last 4 digits.

background: In October 2024, retailer Hot Topic suffered a data breach that exposed 57 million unique email addresses . The impacted data also included physical addresses, phone numbers, purchases, genders, dates of birth and partial credit data containing card type, expiry and last 4 digits.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 56,904,909 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Genders, Names, Partial credit card data, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Purchases, Salutations.
editorial: Fifty-seven million email addresses out of a mall clothing retailer. The figure is wildly out of proportion to the business, and that is the first thing to notice: selling t-shirts does not require a permanent record of who bought what, when, and on which birthday. A loyalty programme is a data business wearing a discount, and the data outlives the customer relationship by years.
The combination here is a working phishing kit rather than a fraud kit. Name, salutation, date of birth, purchase history, and the card type, expiry and last four digits. None of it can be spent.

All of it can be recited, and reciting your last order and the end of your card number is precisely what most people accept as proof that a caller is genuinely from the shop or the bank. That test has not worked for some time, and breaches like this one are why. Partial card data has no value except in being convincing.

Nobody legitimate establishes their identity by reading your own card back to you and then asking for the rest of the number, the expiry date, or a code that has just arrived by text. The institution that issued the card already knows what is on it. Purchases are the field that gives this file its character.

Where a retailer sells band, film and game merchandise, an order history says which fandoms a person follows, and that is a precise hook: a pre-sale for a tour, a limited release or a convention ticket aimed at exactly the right fan is far more tempting than a generic shopping offer.

Treat fan-specific offers that arrive unasked, especially with a deadline, as the likeliest disguise for follow-up phishing. If anyone in your household shopped there as a teenager, the date of birth in the file is worth a conversation about exactly this pattern: a message that knows your name, your birthday and something you bought is still not proof it came from the shop.
Where a younger shopper paid with a parent's card, the partial card details may describe the parent's card rather than the shopper's, so both people should know what to ignore.

The data included 70k unique email addresses along with names, dates of birth, physical addresses, phone numbers, income levels, marital statuses, French social security numbers (NIR) and contact details of relatives or other nominated contacts.
In its disclosure notice, Assurance Retraite attributed the breach to a compromised partner account .
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 70,372 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Family members' names, Government issued IDs, Income levels, Marital statuses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: The people in this set were assistance beneficiaries of France's national pension fund, and the record makes their circumstances plain: income levels and marital statuses sit alongside names, addresses, phone numbers and French social security numbers (NIR). It is hard to design a better list for fraud aimed at vulnerable people.

The field that stands out is the contact details of relatives or other nominated contacts. That turns one person's record into a small family tree, and it enables the scam where a caller claims to be from the pension fund, already knows the beneficiary's details, and asks a son or daughter to help "update the file" or pay a fee to keep the benefit.

The cause, a compromised partner account, is also typical. Large public bodies increasingly share data with service partners, and the partner is often the weaker link. If you or a relative receive support from l'Assurance retraite, treat any call asking for bank details or a fee as fraud. Hang up and call back on the number from an official letter you already have.

The dates add a further warning. The breach occurred in September 2024 and HIBP added the data in October 2026, two years later, and the record counts about 370,000 affected beneficiaries but only 70,000 unique email addresses.

Many of the people in the dataset are older and may not use email at all, which means the follow-up fraud is more likely to arrive by phone or post than by phishing link, and the HIBP count understates how many households are exposed.

A French social security number cannot be changed, and combined with a date of birth and address it supports attempts to open accounts or claim benefits in someone else's name. Relatives who help an older parent manage their paperwork are in a good position to watch for this: unexpected letters from banks, mobile providers or benefits offices are the early sign.
The guide to spotting phishing covers the email side; for phone and post, the rule is the same as above: hang up, and call back on a number you already hold.

The breach exposed 3.2M unique email addresses along with names, genders, dates of birth, phone numbers and approximate geolocations, with the data spanning 2018 to August 2024.
Burger King Russia acknowledged the incident and advised it did not include payment or passport details.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 3,155,792 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
