editorial: The important boundary in this record is a marketing platform. Have I Been Pwned attributes the customer-data exposure to an attack on Mindbox and describes records spanning 2018 to August 2024. A person can appear in an old marketing dataset even if they no longer use the restaurant's account or app.

The addition date in a breach index is also different from the date the incident occurred. The source lists names, contact details, birthdays and approximate location, and reports the company's statement that payment and passport details were not included. That statement should not be expanded into either a guarantee that no other risk exists or a claim that cards were stolen.

The listed fields can help make a fake loyalty reward or account-support message sound personal. This is a risk interpretation, not a report of an observed follow-on scam. If you receive an unexpected reward or account message, open the official app or a known website yourself. A correct name or birthday does not authenticate the sender.

Do not send a one-time code in reply or enter payment details through the message. Report suspicious communication using the service's official support channel and your normal email or device reporting controls. For a company reviewing its own exposure, this case illustrates why account deletion and marketing-data retention need separate questions.

Ask which provider holds historical contact records, what the retention policy covers and how a deletion request propagates to that provider. These are review questions, not a claim about the current Mindbox configuration. The available description does not give the exact intrusion mechanism, so this article leaves that cause unresolved.

The record gives a date range, 2018 to August 2024, which tells you something specific: anyone who signed up for the restaurant's marketing or loyalty programme in those six years may be included, even if they have since deleted the app or changed phone.

Marketing platforms often keep records after the customer relationship ends, which is why a person can be surprised to find themselves in a dataset for a service they stopped using years before. The gap between the August 2024 attack and the September 2026 HIBP date is also long, more than two years.

During that time the data was available to anyone who obtained it, and a birthday and approximate location are fields that do not go out of date. Treat birthday rewards and location-based offers from restaurant brands as the likeliest disguise for a follow-up message, and claim any real reward from inside the app rather than from a link.

background: In August 2024, over 332M rows of email addresses were posted to a popular hacking forum. The post alleged the addresses were scraped from cybersecurity firm SOCRadar, however an investigation on their behalf concluded that "the actor merely utilised functionalities inherent in the platform's standard offerings, designed to gather information from publicly available sources" .
There is no suggestion the incident compromised SOCRadar's security or posed any risk to their customers. In total, the data set contained 282M unique addresses of valid email address format.
how: The post alleged the addresses were scraped from cybersecurity firm SOCRadar, however an investigation on their behalf concluded that "the actor merely utilised functionalities inherent in the platform's standard offerings, designed to gather information from publicly available sources" .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 282,478,425 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses.
editorial: The name given to this entry is the take. It is filed as Not SOCRadar because the forum post claimed a cybersecurity firm had been breached, and the investigation that followed concluded something much duller: the data had been assembled using functionality the platform openly provides, gathering from publicly available sources. No intrusion, no failure, no stolen database.

Claims made while selling something are sales copy, and a hacking forum is a marketplace. Attaching a recognisable company's name to a pile of addresses raises both the price and the attention, and the cost of the claim lands on the company, which then spends weeks proving a negative.

This is why an archive that records what was established separately from what was alleged is worth more than one that repeats the post. If your address is in this set, the proportionate response is almost nothing. It says a mailbox of yours appears in a large scraped aggregate, most likely collected from sources that were already public.

No provider you trusted failed, no password is implicated, and there is nothing to reset. Expect more spam, aimed slightly better. That is the entire consequence, and pretending otherwise would be the same inflation the original post was built on. The record's count also describes the data honestly: 282 million unique addresses "of valid email address format".

That phrase is a reminder that format is not existence. A scraped aggregate of this size will include addresses that were never real, mailboxes that closed years ago and role addresses such as info@ or sales@, which is part of why the number tells you little about how many people are affected. The one practical use of an email-only list is deliverability.

Spam senders use large lists to test which addresses bounce and which do not, then concentrate on the live ones. If you find your address here, a good spam filter and a habit of not replying to or unsubscribing from unknown senders, which confirms the address is read, are the proportionate response.

background: In June 2024, Advance Auto Parts confirmed they had suffered a data breach which was posted for sale to a popular hacking forum. Linked to unauthorised access to Snowflake cloud services, the breach exposed a large number of records related to both customers and employees.
In total, 79M unique email addresses were included in the breach, alongside names, phone numbers, addresses and further data attributes related to company employees.
how: Linked to unauthorised access to Snowflake cloud services, the breach exposed a large number of records related to both customers and employees.
motive: In June 2024, Advance Auto Parts confirmed they had suffered a data breach which was posted for sale to a popular hacking forum.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 79,243,727 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: This belongs to a set rather than standing alone. Through mid-2024 a long run of large companies disclosed breaches traced to their own cloud data warehouse tenants, accounts reached with credentials stolen earlier by malware, on tenants where multi-factor authentication was not enforced. The platform itself was not compromised. The customers' configurations of it were.

It is the clearest illustration available of what shared responsibility means in practice. The provider secures the service; the customer secures access to their instance. Where that line sits is written in documentation nobody reads until a quarter of a billion records have moved, and in 2024 a great many organisations discovered which side of it they had been standing on.

The full case file covers how the campaign worked and why so many companies fell in the same few weeks. The record says the file covered both customers and employees, and those two groups face different problems.
For customers, the fields are the familiar ones: name, email, phone number and postal address, enough for a convincing message about an order, a rewards balance or a recall notice on a car part.

For employees, HIBP notes further attributes related to company staff without listing them, so anyone who worked there should be wary of messages about pay, tax forms or benefits rather than only shopping scams. Auto parts give the phishing a specific shape.

A message about a warranty claim, a part that has been recalled, or a battery or tyre order is believable precisely because so many people buy from a parts chain once or twice a year and do not remember the details.

If you are in this file, treat recall and warranty notices with extra care, and check them against the manufacturer or the official recall service for your country rather than replying to whoever sent the message. The timing is also typical of the 2024 cloud-warehouse cases.
The breach date is 5 June and HIBP added the data on 24 June, after it had already been posted for sale.

When the first public sign of a breach is a sales listing, the people in the data have been exposed for at least as long as the listing has existed, which is why the advice in these cases is always to assume the details are already in use.

background: In May 2024, 2B rows of data with 361M unique email addresses were collated from malicious Telegram channels . The data contained 122GB across 1.7k files with email addresses, usernames, passwords and in many cases, the website they were entered into. The data appears to have been sourced from a combination of existing combolists and info stealer malware.
how: The data appears to have been sourced from a combination of existing combolists and info stealer malware.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 361,468,099 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords, Usernames.
editorial: The detail that sets this collection apart from an ordinary password dump is in the description: in many cases the records include the website the credentials were entered into .

That turns a list of email-and-password pairs into a targeting list, an attacker no longer has to spray a credential across a hundred services hoping for a match, because the file already says where it worked. The other half of the source is information-stealing malware, which changes what the data means for the person in it.

Credentials harvested from an infected device were captured as they were typed. They can include accounts at sites that have never been breached, passwords created after every previous breach notification, and sessions from a browser's saved-password store in one sweep.

So the honest read of an appearance here is: your password is known, possibly with the site it belongs to, and possibly because a machine you used was compromised rather than a company you trusted. Clean the device first if there is any chance it was the source. Then rotate credentials in order of what they can unlock, email before everything, because email resets everything.

A combolist is a text file of email and password pairs, usually stitched together from older breaches, and the record says this collection mixes those with stealer output. That mix matters when you check yourself. An entry could be a password from a breach you already know about and changed years ago, or a credential captured last month from an infected device.

The two call for very different responses, and the only way to tell them apart is to look at whether the password shown is one you still use. The scale also shows how stolen credentials now move. 122GB across 1,700 files, collected from Telegram channels, is a distribution network rather than a breach, and it rewards attackers who automate.

For individuals, that makes two defences more valuable than any single password change: unique passwords per site, so one leaked pair opens one account, and multi-factor sign-in on email and financial accounts, so that a correct password alone is not enough.

background: In May 2024, the conservative news website The Post Millennial suffered a data breach .

The breach resulted in the defacement of the website and links posted to 3 different corpuses of data including hundreds of writers and editors (IP, physical address and email exposed), tens of thousands of subscribers to the site (name, email, username, phone and plain text password exposed), and tens of millions of email addresses from thousands of mailing lists alleged to have been used by The Post Millennial (this has not been independently verified).

The mailing lists appear to be sourced from various campaigns not necessarily run by The Post Millennial and contain a variety of different personal attributes including name, phone and physical address (depending on the campaign). The data was subsequently posted to a popular hacking forum and extensively torrented.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 56,973,345 email addresses are listed in the collection. This does not establish the number of people or service accounts affected.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Genders, IP addresses, Names, Passwords, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Usernames.
editorial: One headline number, three entirely different populations. A few hundred writers and editors had IP addresses and physical addresses exposed. Tens of thousands of subscribers had names, phone numbers and passwords in plain text. The remainder is a far larger list of email addresses. Averaging those into a single figure hides the fact that the worst outcome here belongs to the smallest group.

The staff exposure is not a fraud problem. Home addresses of named writers, published alongside a defacement of the site itself, is targeting, and that is true of any newsroom's staff whatever the outlet publishes and whoever objects to it.

Financial advice does not help with it; the risk is physical, and the remedies are the ones that apply to doxxing rather than to identity theft. For subscribers, passwords stored in plain text in 2024 means exactly what it says: no hashing failed, because none was attempted. Change that password anywhere it was reused, immediately.

And there is a quieter exposure with no remedy at all, appearing on the subscriber list of a political publication discloses something about you that cannot be reset, and that many readers would not have chosen to publish. The mailing-list portion is the largest part of the file and the least certain.

HIBP notes that the lists were alleged to have been used by The Post Millennial, that this has not been independently verified, and that they appear to come from various campaigns not necessarily run by the publication. Anyone who finds their address only in that portion should not conclude they ever subscribed to the site.

They may simply have been on a campaign list that ended up in the same release. The torrenting the record mentions is why this data will not go away. Once a dataset is shared over peer-to-peer networks, it is copied by thousands of people and cannot be withdrawn.

For writers and editors, that permanence is a reason to treat a home address in this file as public from now on, and to consider the measures used for doxxing victims, such as removing the address from data broker sites and asking the local electoral or property register about restricted listings where that option exists.

background: In April 2024, a large trove of data made headlines as having exposed "3 billion people" due to a breach of the National Public Data background check service . The initial corpus of data released in the breach contained billions of rows of personal information, including US social security numbers.

Further partial data sets were later released including extensive personal information and 134M unique email addresses, although the origin and accuracy of the data remains in question. This breach has been flagged as "unverified" and a full description of the incident is in the link above.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 133,957,569 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Genders, Government issued IDs, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: This is the entry that came with the "3 billion people" headline, and it deserves a careful reading because it is flagged as unverified. That flag is not a technicality. Have I Been Pwned's own description says the origin and accuracy of the data remain in question. Billions of rows are not billions of people: rows repeat, and one person can appear many times.

The 134 million unique email addresses here are the more meaningful number. The more important point is what National Public Data was. It was a background check service, a data broker, and most people in its files never had any relationship with it. They did not sign up, accept terms or choose to trust it.

Their names, addresses, dates of birth and US social security numbers were collected and sold about them, then lost. That is why the right response is not a password change. If you are in the US, a credit freeze at all three bureaus is free and stops new accounts being opened in your name, which is the main thing an exposed SSN enables.
It also shows why removing yourself from people search and broker sites is worth the tedious effort: data that is not held cannot leak.

The record dates the breach to April 2024 and the HIBP addition to August 2024, and a background check service typically keeps historical addresses and records, so the details attached to a person may describe where they lived years ago, and the people most affected are those whose social security number is in the file, regardless of whether the address is current.

A credit freeze does not stop every kind of misuse. Tax refund fraud and medical identity fraud use an SSN without opening a credit account. In the US, the IRS offers an Identity Protection PIN that blocks someone else from filing a return in your name, and checking your benefits statements for activity you do not recognise covers the medical side.
Together with a freeze, those are the controls that match what this file actually contains.

background: In early 2024, a large corpus of data from DemandScience (a company owned by Pure Incubation), appeared for sale on a popular hacking forum . Later attributed to a leak from a decommissioned legacy system, the breach contained extensive data that was largely business contact information aggregated from public sources.

Specifically, the data included 122M unique corporate email addresses, physical addresses, phone numbers, employers and job titles. It also included names and for many individuals, a link to their LinkedIn profile.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 121,796,165 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Social media profiles.
editorial: Nobody in this file signed up for anything. DemandScience is a business-to-business marketing data company: the records were aggregated from public and commercial sources into contact profiles, and the people described by them were never customers. The exposure is a by-product of an industry that treats professional identity as inventory. The record also notes the source, a decommissioned legacy system.

That is the most preventable failure mode in this entire archive. A system that has been switched off in the organisational sense but not the technical one has no owner, no patching schedule and no monitoring, while still holding a complete copy of the data it was retired with. Every large company has one.

What makes this data valuable is not its sensitivity but its precision. A name, a corporate email address, a job title and an employer is the exact recipe for business email compromise: it identifies who approves payments, who reports to whom, and who would plausibly receive an instruction from a senior colleague.

If your details are here, the risk lands at work rather than at home, verify payment and account-change requests through a channel you initiated, every time, regardless of how convincing the sender looks.

The record dates the sale to early 2024 and the addition to HIBP to November, but the data itself is older than either date, because a legacy system preserves whatever it held when it was retired. Contact records from an aggregator also tend to include people who have since changed jobs.

That means some entries now point at former employers, and the email addresses involved may already be closed. The people most exposed are those still in the same role, at the same company, with the same direct line.

Because the records were aggregated from public sources, the same people are likely to appear in other B2B lead databases too, and those databases keep being bought, merged and leaked. The step that reduces future exposure is to ask the major B2B data brokers to delete your record and to stop selling it.
Data protection laws in the UK, the EU and several US states give people the right to make that request, and the brokers usually provide an online form.

background: In December 2023, hundreds of gigabytes of data allegedly taken from Indian ISP and digital TV provider Hathway appeared on a popular hacking website . The incident exposed extensive personal information including 4.7M unique email addresses along with names, physical and IP addresses, phone numbers, password hashes and support ticket logs.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 4,670,080 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Device information, Email addresses, IP addresses, Names, Passwords, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Salutations, Support tickets.
editorial: The field that makes this one worse than its size suggests is the last one in the list: support ticket logs. Every other data class here is structured, a name goes in the name box, an address in the address box.

A support ticket is whatever the customer typed while frustrated, which routinely includes account numbers, alternate phone numbers, details about who else lives at the address, and often a password, because people paste them in when asked to describe the problem.

An internet provider also holds a category of data almost nobody else does: the link between a person, a physical address and an IP address over time. That mapping is what turns an IP address found elsewhere into a name, and it is the single most useful record an ISP keeps from an investigative point of view.

For Indian subscribers specifically, the practical risk that follows is the support call that already knows your plan, your address and your last complaint. That is not a coincidence and it is not the provider calling. Device information is another field that sets this record apart.

For a broadband and digital TV provider, that typically means the routers and set-top boxes registered to an account, and it gives a fraudster the vocabulary of a real technician visit: the model of the box, the type of connection, sometimes the installation address.

A call that says your router needs a firmware update, or that a technician must reconfigure your box remotely, sounds plausible when it names the right device. The record says the passwords were stored as hashes but does not describe the algorithm, so the safe assumption is that a weak or reused password could be recovered.

Anyone in the file should change the Hathway account password and any password that shares a pattern with it, and should be firm about one rule: the provider will not ask you to install remote-access software to fix a connection. That request is the most common way a fake support call turns into a takeover of the computer itself.

background: In April 2024, 15M records from the online florist Blooms Today were listed for sale on a popular hacking forum . The most recent data in the breach corpus was from November 2023 and appeared alongside 3.2M unique email addresses, names, phone numbers physical addresses and partial credit card data (card type, 4 digits of the number and expiry date).
The breach did not expose sufficient card data to make purchases. Blooms Today did not respond when contacted about the incident.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In April 2024, 15M records from the online florist Blooms Today were listed for sale on a popular hacking forum .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 3,184,010 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Partial credit card data, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: A florist's database has a property most retail data does not: a large share of the people in it never bought anything. Gift orders carry a recipient, a name, an address, often a phone number, belonging to somebody who has no account, agreed to no terms, and will never receive a notification because the company has no relationship with them to notify.
Whether this particular corpus separates buyers from recipients is not something the breach record can tell you, and it is worth being precise about that rather than assuming the worst.

What the record does say is that 3.2 million addresses appeared alongside names, phone numbers, physical addresses and partial card data, in a file offered for sale roughly five months after the most recent data in it was created. Nobody was watching in between. The exposure that follows is a delivery scam, and flowers make it unusually effective.

An unexpected delivery is plausible for almost anyone, confirming an address for one feels harmless, and a message that already has your address and the last four digits of a card reads as legitimate. A courier that cannot deliver does not need your card details to try again, and a florist does not ask for them by text.

The record also notes that Blooms Today did not respond when contacted about the incident. That leaves people in the file without the usual next steps from a company notice, such as an explanation of what was taken, an offer of monitoring, or a contact for questions.

When a company is silent, the HIBP record is often the most complete public account of what happened, and the safest reading is the full field list. Gift-giving is also seasonal. Florists see peaks around specific holidays, and a delivery scam timed to one of those dates has an even better chance of being believed.

If you are in this file, or if you regularly receive flowers, a sensible rule is to treat any request for payment or card details that arrives with a delivery notice as fraud, and to contact the sender of the gift directly if something seems to be stuck.

background: In August 2023, PlayCyberGames which "allows users to play any games with LAN function or games using IP address" suffered a data breach which exposed 3.7M customer records. The data included email addresses, usernames and MD5 password hashes with a constant value in the "salt" field. PlayCyberGames did not respond to multiple attempts to disclose the breach.

editorial: The detail that matters is six words long: MD5 hashes with a constant value in the salt field. A salt that never changes is not a salt. Its entire function is to be different for every record, so that two people who chose the same password do not produce the same hash and one precomputed table cannot be run against the whole file.

Fix the value and you have plain MD5 with extra steps. What makes this instructive rather than merely bad is that it passes inspection. The column exists. The field is populated. The word "salt" appears in the schema, in the code, and presumably in whatever security questionnaire the company answered.

Everything is present except the property that made any of it worth doing, which is a far more common shape of failure than having no protection at all. The last line of the record is the one with consequences for readers: multiple attempts to disclose the breach went unanswered.

No reset emails were sent, no notice was published, and 3.7 million people were never told by the company that lost their credentials. If a password from a gaming account of yours is still in use somewhere else, this is the only notification you are going to get. The service itself explains who is likely to be in the file.

A tool that "allows users to play any games with LAN function or games using IP address" is built for people who want to play local-network games over the internet, which means players of older or modded games, often young, often using the same username across gaming communities.

A username in this file is therefore a good pivot to other accounts, and an unsalted-in-practice MD5 hash is a weak guard on a password that was probably reused there too. Tools of this kind also tend to ask for network access and run in the background, so it is worth checking whether the client is still installed on any machine you use.

Software from a company that did not answer breach reports is unlikely to be receiving careful security updates either. Removing it, and changing any password that matched the one used for the account, closes both doors at once.

background: In April 2023, the stolen identity marketplace Genesis Market was shut down by the FBI and a coalition of law enforcement agencies across the globe in "Operation Cookie Monster" . The service traded in "browser fingerprints" which enabled criminals to impersonate victims and access their online services.

As many of the impacted accounts did not include email addresses, "8M" is merely an approximation intended to indicate scale. Other personal data compromised by the service included names, addresses and credit card information, although not all individuals had each of these fields exposed.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 8,000,000 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Browser user agent details, Credit card CVV, Credit cards, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Names, Passwords, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Usernames.
editorial: Genesis Market is the entry in this archive that best explains why changing your password is sometimes not enough. The service did not primarily trade passwords: it traded browser fingerprints and session cookies, the tokens that tell a website you have already logged in, bundled with enough device detail to make the impersonation look like your own machine.

A buyer could load that package and appear to a service as the victim, on the victim's apparent device, already authenticated. No password prompt, and in many cases no two-factor challenge either, because the session had already passed it. This is why security advice increasingly includes "sign out of all sessions everywhere" after a compromise, which is a control most people have never used.

The other thing to take from this record is where the data came from. Genesis Market's inventory was harvested from infected consumer devices, which means the victims were compromised personally rather than through any company they dealt with. The site was taken down in a coordinated international operation in 2023, and the underlying trade did not stop, the marketplaces changed names.

If you are in this file, treat the device as the problem rather than the account. Clean or rebuild it, then revoke active sessions on your important services, then change passwords, in that order, because doing it the other way round means handing your new password to whatever is still watching.

The record is explicit that "8M" is an approximation intended to indicate scale, because many of the compromised accounts did not include email addresses. That means checking an email address can miss people who were in the market's inventory: a victim whose stolen bot record held only cookies and browser data, with no email field, would not appear in a search by address at all.

If you had a malware infection around 2022 or early 2023, the cautious response applies whether or not your address appears. The record also lists credit card numbers and CVVs among the compromised data, which is unusual in this archive. Card data captured from an infected browser is complete enough to spend, unlike the partial card data in retail breaches.

Anyone who saved cards in a browser on a machine that was later found to be infected should ask their bank to reissue those cards, because a CVV in criminal hands removes the last check an online merchant relies on.

background: In July 2024, the Indian stock brokerage firm Angel One confirmed that data leaked online related to a breach that occurred in April 2023 . The leaked data included 7.9M user records containing 6.8M unique email addresses, along with names, physical addresses, phone numbers, bank account numbers, Permanent Account Numbers (PANs) and portfolio holdings.
Angel One emphasised that the breach "has no impact on client securities, funds, or credentials".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 6,765,054 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Bank account numbers, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Financial investments, Government issued IDs, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Angel One's statement that the breach "has no impact on client securities, funds, or credentials" is probably accurate as far as it goes, and it misses the point. Nobody needs your trading password to misuse this data. The set pairs names, phone numbers and addresses with bank account numbers, PANs and portfolio holdings, which is a complete brief for an investment scam.

India's stock-market fraud of the moment is the fake trading group: a WhatsApp or Telegram contact posing as a broker's research desk, offering tips or an "institutional" app, then taking deposits. A caller who can quote your real holdings and your PAN is far more persuasive than one guessing, and this leak supplies exactly that. Note the dates too.
The breach happened in April 2023 and was confirmed in July 2024, more than a year later. The data had plenty of time to circulate before anyone was told.

If you held an Angel One account in that period, treat any unsolicited contact about your portfolio as fraudulent unless you started it, and never move money to an account a caller gives you, however much they know. The record's three dates tell the story in order: the breach in April 2023, the confirmation in July 2024, and the addition to HIBP in October 2026.

Each step happened long after the previous one, and an account holder checking today is looking at data that has been usable for more than three years. Portfolio holdings change, but a PAN, a bank account number and a home address mostly do not, so age reduces the value of this data much less than it would for a password list.

Market regulators in India publish warnings about unregistered investment advisers and fake trading apps, and the safest habit is to check any adviser or platform against the regulator's own register before engaging. Brokers do not run stock-tip groups on messaging apps or ask clients to install a separate app to receive "institutional" allocations.
If you were contacted by someone who knew your holdings, report it to the broker through its official support channel, and do not continue the conversation where it started.

background: In March 2023, data allegedly taken from СберСпасибо (SberSpasibo), the loyalty program of Russian bank Сбербанк (Sberbank), was published online . The data contained records relating to 48M users, including 3.3M unique email addresses alongside phone numbers and dates of birth.
Data also included bank card numbers stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, plus loyalty program details such as membership dates and the redemption of bonus points for partner offers.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 3,288,711 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Bank card numbers, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Loyalty program details, Phone numbers.
editorial: The detail worth understanding here is how the card numbers were stored: as unsalted SHA-1 hashes. That sounds protective, and for passwords it would at least slow an attacker down. For card numbers it does very little.

A card number is a short string with a known structure: the first six digits identify the issuer, the last digit is a checksum, and only the digits in between vary. That is a small enough space to hash every possibility and match the results, so a hashed card number should be treated as an exposed one.

The rest of the record is a loyalty program's view of a person: phone number, date of birth, email, membership dates and which partner offers they redeemed bonus points on. Loyalty data looks trivial but it is behavioural, and it is the kind of detail that makes a fake bank call sound real ("we noticed an unusual redemption on your Spasibo account").

The data was published in March 2023 and reached Have I Been Pwned in November 2026, so it has had years to be used. If you are a Sberbank customer in this set, the card you held then should be reissued if it has not been already.
The record counts 48 million users but only 3.3 million unique email addresses, which tells you that most people in the loyalty programme are identified by phone number rather than email.

For them, the realistic follow-up is a call or text rather than a phishing email, and phone numbers attached to a date of birth are the details a fake bank security service asks a customer to confirm before talking them into a "safe account" transfer.
The gap between the March 2023 publication and the November 2026 HIBP date also limits what checking an email can tell you.

Anyone who was a Spasibo member in 2023, whether or not their email appears here, should treat calls that mention bonus points or partner offers as unverified, and should call the bank back on the number printed on the card rather than on any number given during the call.

background: In February 2023, data alleged to have been taken from the fraud protection service Eye4Fraud was listed for sale on a popular hacking forum .

Spanning tens of millions of rows with 16M unique email addresses, the data was spread across 147 tables totalling 65GB and included both direct users of the service and what appears to be individuals who'd placed orders on other services that implemented Eye4Fraud to protect their sales.

The data included names and bcrypt password hashes for users, and names, phone numbers, physical addresses and partial credit card data (card type and last 4 digits) for orders placed using the service. Eye4Fraud did not respond to multiple attempts to report the incident.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In February 2023, data alleged to have been taken from the fraud protection service Eye4Fraud was listed for sale on a popular hacking forum .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 16,000,591 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, IP addresses, Names, Partial credit card data, Passwords, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: There is an unavoidable irony in a fraud prevention service losing its data, but the mechanism is the more interesting part. The records include both direct users of the service and people who simply placed orders with merchants that used it. Most of the second group had no idea the company existed, and no way to find out.

This is what a verification layer does structurally: to check whether an order is fraudulent, it has to receive the order, the name, the address, the phone number, the partial card data. Hundreds of merchants send that in, and it accumulates in one place.

The service is doing exactly what it was hired to do, and in doing so becomes a far more attractive target than any individual shop it protects. 147 tables across 65GB also tells you something about how this data was kept. That is a warehouse, not a working set, years of retained transaction context long past the point where it could inform a fraud decision.

The defensible version of this business holds each record for as long as the check requires and deletes it afterwards. For anyone in the file: the partial card data is not spendable, but it is persuasive. A caller who can recite the last four digits and your address sounds like your bank precisely because most people treat those details as proof.
They are not proof; they are in this file. The record notes that Eye4Fraud did not respond to multiple attempts to report the incident.

For the people whose orders were screened by the service, that silence is compounded by distance: the merchant they bought from may never have learned that its order data was part of the leak, so no notice reached them through that route either. The HIBP entry may be the only notification most of them ever receive.

The direct users of the service, merchants and their staff, are a separate group in the data, with bcrypt-hashed passwords. Bcrypt makes those passwords slow to crack, but the accounts belonged to people who make fraud decisions for online shops, and a convincing message from the "fraud review team" asking them to approve, release or re-route orders is the business version of the consumer scam.
Merchants in the file should confirm any change to fraud rules or payout details inside the dashboard they log into themselves.

background: In December 2022, India’s government-approved online travel agency RailYatri suffered a data breach . The incident impacted over 31M customers and exposed 23M unique email addresses. Also impacted were names, genders, phone numbers and tickets purchased, including travel information and fares.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 23,209,732 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Genders, Names, Phone numbers, Purchases.
editorial: No passwords, no payment data, no identity documents, by the standards of this archive the field list is mild. The travel data is what makes it worth reading carefully anyway. Tickets purchased, with routes and fares, is a movement history: where a person goes, how often, in which class, and on which dates.

For most passengers that is a privacy loss rather than a security one. For some it is not. A record of regular journeys between two towns identifies where someone lives and where they work, or who they visit, with a precision that no amount of careful social media hygiene would have given away.

Anyone who has moved away from a person they needed to get away from should treat that as the real exposure here. The immediate practical risk, though, is phone-based. A name, a mobile number and a genuine recent booking is everything a convincing scam call needs, refunds for cancelled trains, fare adjustments, seat upgrades, all referencing a journey the recipient actually took.
Indian users in particular have seen sustained campaigns of exactly this shape. No travel operator resolves a refund by asking for a one-time code or a UPI approval; anyone who does is stealing.

The record counts more than 31 million affected customers but 23 million unique email addresses, so several million people are in the data without an email at all, most likely identified by phone number alone. For those passengers the exposure arrives by SMS and phone call, the channels Indian train travellers already use for PNR updates, platform changes and refund notices.

A scam that imitates those messages does not have to teach anyone a new habit. Fares and travel class are a quieter detail with their own use. They sketch a spending level and a routine, which helps a fraudster decide who is worth a longer con.

For frequent travellers, the safest habit is to check any refund or booking change in the official app or on the railway's own site, and to remember that a refund never requires you to approve a payment request on your UPI app, because approving a request sends money out rather than bringing it in.

background: In July 2022, the Chinese adult website Hjedd was found to be leaking more than 13M customer records which subsequently appeared on a popular hacking forum . The exposed data included email and IP addresses, usernames and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes.

editorial: The passwords here were stored as bcrypt hashes, which is the right answer, slow by design, salted per record, still holding up. It makes almost no difference to the people in this file, because the password was never the damaging part. The damaging part is an email address appearing next to the name of an adult website.

That is what the sensitive flag on this entry means, and why those entries behave unlike the rest of the archive. Everywhere else, exposure creates a task you can complete: change this, freeze that, watch a statement. Here the harm is the disclosure itself, and disclosure has no undo. A password can be rotated.

Membership of a site cannot be un-leaked, and the IP addresses alongside it narrow down where the account was used. The predictable consequence is extortion mail, and knowing where the accurate details came from is what defuses it.

A message quoting the real site name, sometimes a real old password, is designed to make the rest of the claim credible, and the rest of the claim is invented. There are no recordings; there is a breach file with your address in it, bought for a few dollars.

Replying or paying proves the mailbox is live, and that is the only thing the sender learns. The record dates the exposure to July 2022 and the HIBP addition to October 2023, more than a year later, and says the data was found leaking before it appeared on a hacking forum.

That sequence is typical of misconfigured databases: the data is readable by anyone who finds it, and copies are taken before the owner notices. For people in the file, the time since then means extortion mail referencing this site can arrive at any point, often years after the event, which makes it easy to mistake for a new incident.

Because the entry is flagged as sensitive, HIBP only shows it to a person who has verified ownership of the address. That is worth knowing if you search for someone else's address and see nothing: the absence does not mean they are not in it.

background: In May 2022, the survey website QuestionPro was the target of an extortion attempt relating to an alleged data breach . Over 100GB of data containing 22M unique email addresses (some of which appear to be generated by the platform), are alleged to have been extracted from the service along with IP addresses, browser user agents and results relating to surveys.

QuestionPro would not confirm whether a breach had occurred (although they did confirm they were the target of an extortion attempt), so the data was initially flagged as "unverified". Subsequent verification by impacted HIBP subscribers later led to the removal of the unverified flag.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: QuestionPro would not confirm whether a breach had occurred (although they did confirm they were the target of an extortion attempt), so the data was initially flagged as "unverified".
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 22,229,637 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Browser user agent details, Email addresses, IP addresses, Survey results.
editorial: "Survey results" is the quietest data class in this archive and one of the most revealing. People answer surveys candidly precisely because they believe the answers are aggregated and anonymous. Tie those answers back to an email address and an IP address, as this data does, and the assumption that made them candid is the thing that makes the file valuable.

The employee engagement survey, the health questionnaire, the political polling, the customer satisfaction form that asked why you left, all of it is opinion given under an expectation of distance from the person holding it. Worth noting too how this record's status changed.

It sat flagged as unverified because the company would not confirm a breach, and the flag was removed only after people found their own accurate records in it. A company declining to confirm does not make a dataset false, and the verification eventually came from the people in it rather than from the organisation holding it.
HIBP also notes that some of the email addresses appear to have been generated by the platform itself.

That detail matters for anyone checking their own address: a survey service may create placeholder or anonymised respondent identifiers, so the presence of an odd-looking address in the count does not inflate the real exposure much, while the presence of your own address means a survey you answered was linked to you more directly than the form suggested.

Two of the fields, IP addresses and browser user agents, are the technical fingerprint of the moment someone submitted a response. For most respondents that is low risk on its own. For anyone who answered a workplace survey from an office network, it can be enough to tie an "anonymous" response back to a team or a building.

If you have ever answered a sensitive survey run through a third-party tool, this is a reminder to read the anonymity promise as a statement about the report the organiser sees, not about what the platform itself stores.

The breach exposed names, email addresses, genders, social media account identities, auth tokens from social logins and passwords stored as salted MD5 hashes. editorial: Two things in this record matter more than the 23 million total. The first is salted MD5 password hashing, which is a 1990s answer to a 2022 problem: the salt prevents one cracking run solving every shared password, but MD5 is fast enough that ordinary hardware grinds through common passwords regardless. Anything that appears in a wordlist should be considered recovered.
The second is the auth tokens from social logins. Those are not passwords, they are the credentials a site holds so it can act against the account you signed in with.

Their value to an attacker depends entirely on what scope was granted and whether the tokens are still valid, which is why "revoke third-party app access" belongs on the response list alongside "change your password". Most people have never opened that settings page and would be surprised by what is on it.

The note that the company did not respond to repeated contact attempts is worth registering too. A breach where the operator is unreachable means no notification, no forced password reset, and no invalidation of those tokens, so the only person who can act is the user.

If you had an account here, go into the social account you used to sign in and revoke the connection yourself. The record says the service was based in Hong Kong, dates the breach to May 2022, and shows the data reaching HIBP in July, about two months later.

Readers of serialised manga and web comics on a mobile app are often young, and many sign in with a social account rather than creating a password, which is why the auth tokens matter more here than in most breaches: for those users the token, not the password, was the credential. Social sign-in is also why the "social media account identities" field deserves attention.

It links an anonymous reading account to a named profile on another platform. Anyone who read under a separate identity on purpose should assume that link is now known, and the useful step is the one the take already describes: open the social account's connected apps page, remove Mangatoon, and remove any other app there you no longer use.

background: In early 2022, a collective known as IT Army whose stated goal is to "completely de-anonymise most Russian users by leaking hundreds of gigabytes of databases" published over 30GB of data allegedly sourced from Russian courier service CDEK. The data contained over 19M unique email addresses along with names and phone numbers.
The authenticity of the breach could not be independently established and has been flagged as "unverified".

editorial: This is one of the few entries in the archive flagged as unverified, and that flag is the reason it is worth reading. The data was published by a hacktivist collective during a war, with the stated aim of de-anonymising Russian internet users at scale, and its authenticity could not be independently established.

It is filed as what it is: an allegation with 19 million addresses attached. Politically motivated dumps fail differently from criminal ones. A seller has a commercial interest in the data being genuine, because buyers who get fabricated files do not come back.

A collective publishing to cause harm to a population has an interest in publication itself, accuracy is a secondary concern, and mixing authentic records with assembled ones costs them nothing and is nearly impossible to disprove from outside. Both readings carry real risk, which is the uncomfortable part.

Courier records are home addresses and delivery histories, about as sensitive as consumer data gets; and for people living under a government that may take an interest in who appears in a hostile dump, being listed is its own hazard whether or not the row is real. Treat an unverified appearance as neither proof that you were breached nor evidence that you were not.

The fields that were published are limited to names, email addresses and phone numbers, and the record does not list delivery addresses even though a courier would hold them. That gap is a reason not to assume the worst in either direction: either the publishers released only part of what they had, or the data was assembled from a narrower source than its label suggests.

The unverified flag covers both possibilities. For people outside Russia who used CDEK to receive parcels, the practical exposure is ordinary: phone numbers and names in a widely shared dump attract spam and delivery-themed scams. For people inside Russia, the more relevant question is what association with any leaked dataset might mean in their situation, and that is a judgement only they can make.
Changing a password does not affect either risk, because none was published.

background: In approximately August 2021, hundreds of gigabytes of business data collated from public sources was obtained and later published to a popular hacking forum . Sourced from a customer of Bureau van Dijk's (BvD) "Orbis" product, the corpus of data released contained hundreds of millions of lines about corporations and individuals, including personal information such as names and dates of birth.

The data also included 28M unique email addresses along with physical addresses (presumedly corporate locations), phone numbers and job titles. There was no unauthorised access to BvD's systems, nor did the incident expose any of their or parent company's Moody's clients.
how: There was no unauthorised access to BvD's systems, nor did the incident expose any of their or parent company's Moody's clients.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 27,917,714 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

editorial: Nobody in this file has a relationship with the company named at the top of it. Personal details were collated from public sources into Bureau van Dijk's Orbis product, Orbis was licensed to customers, and the leak came from one of those customers. Three hops between the person and the breach, and the person chose none of them.

That is the structural failure of the data broker economy rather than a lapse by anyone in particular. Aggregation is the entire product: a name in one register, a date of birth in a filing, a job title on a third site are individually public and individually useless, and combining them into a profile is what the customer is paying for.

Once assembled, the profile copies perfectly and ends up exactly as secure as the least careful licensee. The vendor can be faultless and the outcome identical. Which is why "sourced from public information" reassures less than it is meant to.

Nothing here can be withdrawn at source, because none of it was private to begin with, and there is no account to close, no consent to revoke, and no notification obligation to anyone whose dossier was compiled without their involvement. The exposure is the collation, and the collation is the business.

The record presumes that the physical addresses are mostly corporate locations, but it lists dates of birth among the fields, which is personal data in any context. Company directors and officers are the people most likely to be described by both, because their details appear in public filings that business databases collect.

For them, a convincing approach can combine a correct date of birth, a correct company role and a correct office address. That combination supports a specific kind of fraud: requests that appear to come from a company registry, a bank's business team or a regulator, asking a director to confirm details or pay a fee to keep a filing current.
Directors in this file should check any such request against the registry's own website, and should know that many official registries publish warnings about exactly these letters and emails.

background: During the first half of 2021, LinkedIn was targeted by attackers who scraped data from hundreds of millions of public profiles and later sold them online . Whilst the scraping did not constitute a data breach nor did it access any personal data not intended to be publicly accessible, the data was still monetised and later broadly circulated in hacking circles.

The scraped data contains approximately 400M records with 125M unique email addresses, as well as names, geographic locations, genders and job titles. LinkedIn specifically addresses the incident in their post on An update on report of scraped data .

Whilst the scraping did not constitute a data breach nor did it access any personal data not intended to be publicly accessible, the data was still monetised and later broadly circulated in hacking circles.
The scraped data contains approximately 400M records with 125M unique email addresses, as well as names, geographic locations, genders and job titles.
LinkedIn specifically addresses the incident in their post on An update on report of scraped data .

editorial: Have I Been Pwned describes this collection as scraped public profile data, not a breach of private LinkedIn data. That distinction matters when explaining how the records were obtained, even though their collection and circulation can still create privacy concerns. The profile you made public was made public one reader at a time.

That is a different thing from public data collected at scale and circulated. HIBP's record describes approximately 400 million records and 125 million unique email addresses; the two counts are not counts of individual people. Aggregated contact and employment details can help make phishing messages more targeted.

This is the same argument that runs through the 2021 Facebook scrape and the Clearview AI case file . Public and harmless are not the same word, and scale is what separates them. The field list explains why this collection keeps reappearing in other compilations.
Job titles, education levels and locations are exactly what a recruiter, a salesperson or an attacker wants when deciding who to approach and how.

A file that ties those to an email address lets someone sort 125 million addresses by seniority, sector and city, which is the first step in picking a target for a fake job offer, an invoice fraud aimed at a finance team, or a message that pretends to come from a colleague. That use is the realistic risk for most people in it.

The well-worn pattern after professional-network scrapes is a recruiter message for a role that matches your title a little too well, followed by a request to move the conversation to another app, open a document, or complete a "skills test" that installs something. Because the details in the approach are accurate, they read as research rather than as a warning sign.

Unlike most entries in this archive, part of the fix is in your own hands, because the source was profile data you chose to publish. LinkedIn's privacy settings let you limit what is visible to people outside your network and to search engines.
Narrowing that does nothing about copies already circulating, but it does reduce what the next scrape collects, and the next one is the one you can still influence.

breaches.summary: In April 2021, 13TB of compromised Domino's India appeared for sale on a hacking forum after which the company acknowledged a major data breach they dated back to March. background: In April 2021, 13TB of compromised Domino's India appeared for sale on a hacking forum after which the company acknowledged a major data breach they dated back to March. The compromised data included 22.5 million unique email addresses, names, phone numbers, order histories and physical addresses.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 22,527,655 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Purchases.
editorial: An order history attached to a delivery address and a phone number is not retail data, it is a behavioural record. Where you live, roughly when you are home, how often you order, how much you spend and how many people you are ordering for. Twenty-two and a half million of those, from a company most customers thought of as a way to get dinner.

What made this breach notorious in India was what happened after it: a public search interface was built on top of the data, so that anyone could type a phone number and read back the orders and addresses attached to it. That step is the one worth remembering.

A dump on a forum has a small audience with some technical patience; a search box has everybody. The same records become a different kind of danger when the barrier drops from "can navigate a hacking forum" to "can type". The fraud that follows is the refund call, and it works because the caller opens with a real order.

Something went wrong with your last delivery, we are processing a refund, approve the request on your phone. No merchant in India or anywhere else returns money by asking you to approve a UPI collect request or read out a one-time code, a refund travels back along the payment that made it, with nothing required from you.

The record says 13TB of data appeared for sale in April 2021 and that the company dated the breach to March, which is a short gap between intrusion and sale. Food delivery data also stays accurate for a long time.

People rarely move house as often as they order dinner, so an address and phone number from 2021 are still a reasonable guess at where many customers live today, which is why this breach keeps its value years after the event. Delivery addresses also include workplaces, hostels and family homes, and the name on an order is not always the person who lives there.

If you ordered for others, or others ordered to your address, more than one person in your household may receive calls that reference the same order history. A household rule that nobody shares a one-time code or approves a payment request in response to an inbound call covers everyone at once.

background: In March 2021, the world's largest eyewear company Luxoticca suffered a data breach via one of their partners that exposed the personal information of more than 70M people . The data was subsequently sold via a popular hacking forum in late 2022 and included email and physical addresses, names, genders, dates of birth and phone numbers.
In a statement from Luxottica, they advised they were aware of the incident and are currently "considering other notification obligations".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 77,093,812 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Genders, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Two details in this record deserve more attention than the headline number. The first is that it happened through a partner, which meant the 70 million people in the file had no relationship with the company whose name is on it, they bought glasses from a brand Luxottica owns, or had an eye test at an optician it supplies. The second is the interval.

The intrusion dates to March 2021. The data was sold on a hacking forum in late 2022. For roughly eighteen months the exposure existed and there was nothing for anyone in it to read, act on or be notified about. A company's statement that it is "considering other notification obligations" is the sound that gap makes. Nothing in the exposed fields can be changed.

Name, date of birth, address, phone number and gender are the permanent identifiers, and the practical consequence is a phone call, some years later, from somebody who already knows all five. The partner route also explains why many people in this file will not recognise the name on the record.

Luxottica sits behind a long list of eyewear brands and optical retailers, so the person whose details leaked may only ever have dealt with a high-street optician or an online glasses shop. If you received a notice and thought it was a mistake because you have never heard of Luxottica, it may not be. The relationship ran through a brand you did know.

That indirection has a practical edge. Scam messages after this kind of breach can name any of the brands in the group, or a generic "vision insurance" or "eye care" provider, and still sound plausible to someone who has had an eye test in the last few years.

A date of birth and phone number on file are also what an insurance or benefits fraudster needs to sound legitimate. The defence is unglamorous: do not confirm personal details to inbound callers about prescriptions, insurance claims or refunds, and check any such contact against the provider whose receipt or card you actually hold.

The data was obtained sometime in 2021 by abusing an API that enabled email addresses to be resolved to Twitter profiles. The subsequent results were then composed into a corpus of data containing email addresses alongside public Twitter profile information including names, usernames and follower counts.

editorial: This one is dangerous for a reason the account count does not convey. The API that was abused resolved an email address to a profile. The resulting file therefore does something no ordinary credential dump does: it links a pseudonymous handle to a real email address. For most people that is an annoyance.

For anyone whose account was deliberately separated from their identity, someone posting under a pseudonym about a government, an employer, an abusive partner, a religion they left, or a diagnosis, it is the specific harm they built the separation to prevent. The link is not reversible, the file is public, and a password change does nothing about it.

If that applies to you, the useful response is not account hygiene. It is to check which email address the pseudonymous account was registered with, assume the connection is known, and decide whether the account should continue under that identity at all. The dates in the record show how long a quiet exposure can last.

The API abuse took place in 2021, and the corpus surfaced on a hacking forum in early 2023, roughly two years later. Throughout that time the linkage between handles and email addresses existed in private hands, and nothing visible to the account holders had changed.

That is why the absence of passwords in the field list should not be read as the absence of harm: the fields that are present (email, name, username and follower counts) are the ones that describe who someone is and how much reach they have. Follower counts deserve a sentence of their own.
They let anyone sort two hundred million rows by influence, which turns a general file into a list of journalists, officials, creators and brand accounts with the email address behind each one.

Accounts like those are the targets of fake verification notices, fake copyright strikes and fake partnership offers, all of which work better when the sender knows the real address the account was registered with.
If you run a large account, the practical step is to make sure that address is not one you publish anywhere, and to move the account to an address used for nothing else.

background: In November 2020, a collection of more than 23,000 allegedly breached websites known as Cit0day were made available for download on several hacking forums . The data consisted of 226M unique email address alongside password pairs, often represented as both password hashes and the cracked, plain text versions. Independent verification of the data established it contains many legitimate, previously undisclosed breaches.
The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com .
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 226,883,414 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: Twenty-three thousand websites. That number is the whole story, because almost none of them are sites you would remember using. The forum you joined once in 2013, the shop that sold one thing you needed, the local club, the game that shut down, small sites with small security budgets, breached individually and unremarkably, then swept into one collection. Nobody notified anyone.

Most of those sites never knew, and a good number no longer existed by the time the collection was published. There is no company here to be accountable, no disclosure statement, and no reset email coming. The compilation also carried cracked plain-text passwords alongside the hashes, which removes the last bit of friction.

If you find yourself in this one, the question is not which site leaked it, that is usually unanswerable, but where else that password was ever used. That is the only question this data makes it possible to act on. The record flags this collection as unverified, and that status is honest rather than reassuring.

With twenty-three thousand sources, nobody could check each one against the site it supposedly came from. Independent analysis found many genuine, previously undisclosed breaches inside it, which means the right reading for an individual is simple: if your address and a password you recognise appear together, the pairing is real whether or not the site it came from can ever be named.

A compilation of small sites also changes who is exposed. Large companies tend to force password resets after a breach. A defunct forum or a one-person shop does not, so the passwords in this file were never invalidated at the source, and many of the accounts still exist in some form.

The useful exercise is a short inventory: which old services might still have an account under that email, which of them hold anything that matters, and which can simply be deleted. Our guide to auditing a digital footprint walks through finding forgotten accounts, and every deleted account is one less place an old password can be tried.

background: In October 2020, a security researcher published a technique for scraping large volumes of data from Gravatar, the service for providing globally unique avatars . 167 million names, usernames and MD5 hashes of email addresses used to reference users' avatars were subsequently scraped and distributed within the hacking community.

114 million of the MD5 hashes were cracked and distributed alongside the source hash, thus disclosing the original email address and accompanying data. Following the impacted email addresses being searchable in HIBP, Gravatar release an FAQ detailing the incident .
how: In October 2020, a security researcher published a technique for scraping large volumes of data from Gravatar, the service for providing globally unique avatars .
167 million names, usernames and MD5 hashes of email addresses used to reference users' avatars were subsequently scraped and distributed within the hacking community.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 113,990,759 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Usernames.
editorial: There is a design lesson buried in this record that outlives the incident. Gravatar identified users by the MD5 hash of their email address, published in the page source of every site that showed an avatar. The reasoning was reasonable at the time: a hash is not the address, so the address is not being disclosed. It does not hold.

MD5 is fast, email addresses follow predictable patterns, and the total space of plausible addresses is small enough to work through. Of 167 million scraped hashes, 114 million were reversed to the original address. Hashing an identifier that an attacker can guess is not anonymisation; it is a lookup table waiting to be built.

Nothing sensitive was stored and nothing was stolen in the conventional sense, this was scraping a service that was answering exactly as designed. The exposure is the mapping itself: a name, a username and the email address behind it, for a hundred million people who had only ever wanted a profile picture to follow them between websites.

Gravatar's own FAQ about the incident, which HIBP links to, is a good example of a service explaining scraping clearly rather than calling it a breach. The data was collectable because the service answered public requests as designed.

That distinction does not change much for the people in the file, but it changes what to ask of similar services: whether identifiers exposed in public pages can be reversed, and whether the service rate-limits the kind of bulk enumeration this needed. For individuals the residual risk is linkage.

If you commented on blogs or forums that used Gravatar, the same avatar and username appeared across those sites, and this file connects them to an email address. Anyone who kept a pseudonymous blog identity separate from a work address should check which email is attached to their Gravatar account.
Moving the avatar to an address used for nothing else, or removing it, stops new pages from repeating the link.

background: In September 2020, the Nitro PDF service suffered a massive data breach which exposed over 70 million unique email addresses . The breach also exposed names, bcrypt password hashes and the titles of converted documents. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com .

editorial: The record mentions it almost in passing, and it is the most interesting thing in the entry: alongside the addresses and the bcrypt hashes, the breach exposed the titles of converted documents. Not the documents themselves. Their names. File names are content, written by people who assumed no one else would ever read them.

"Offer letter final signed", "divorce petition draft 3", "Series A term sheet", "biopsy results", "redundancy list Q4". Nobody names a private file euphemistically for their own benefit. A list of what seventy-seven million people were converting to PDF is therefore a map of what they were doing, legal trouble, job moves, medical news, deals in progress, indexed by email address and dated.

For companies that is targeting material of unusual quality: knowing an organisation converted a term sheet or a redundancy list in a particular week tells an attacker which pretext to use and exactly when to send it. For individuals it is an inference problem with no remedy. The password can be changed, and bcrypt probably held it anyway.

The title of a document you converted five years ago cannot be renamed after the fact. The record says the data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com, a breach search service, rather than disclosed by the company with an affected-user list.

That is common for older breaches and it affects how people find out: there was no reliable notification path for seventy million users of a PDF tool, many of whom signed up once to convert a single file. Checking an address is often the only way anyone in this file will learn they were included.
A single-use account like that is exactly the kind people forget, and forgotten accounts are where old passwords stay valid.

If you appear here, the useful steps are to change the password if it was reused anywhere, and to think about which document titles from that period might be sensitive if read by a stranger, particularly anything relating to employment, legal matters or deals, because those are the subjects a targeted email would most plausibly reference.
