background: In June 2020, the user-generated stories website Wattpad suffered a huge data breach that exposed almost 270 million records . The data was initially sold then published on a public hacking forum where it was broadly shared. The incident exposed extensive personal information including names and usernames, email and IP addresses, genders, birth dates and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 268,765,495 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Bios, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Genders, Geographic locations, IP addresses, Names, Passwords, Social media profiles, User website URLs, Usernames.
editorial: The passwords were bcrypt hashes, which is the right answer and means the credential risk here is comparatively low. The exposure that matters is everything else, and it is unusually personal for a breach of this size. Wattpad is a writing community with a young user base, and the file includes bios, dates of birth, genders, geographic locations and links to users' other social profiles.

A bio is freely written text in which people describe themselves, often, at that age, more candidly than they would on any form. Combined with a date of birth and a location, it produces a record that identifies a person who was a minor at the time and says something about who they were.

That kind of data does not age out of being sensitive; it just stops being accurate. Anyone who wrote on the platform as a teenager and has since built a separate adult identity should check whether the linked social profiles in this file still connect the two.

The field list includes IP addresses and user website URLs alongside the profile fields, and that extends the linkage beyond the platform. A personal website or a link to another social profile is exactly what a writer adds to be found by readers.

In a breach it becomes a map from a pen name to the rest of someone's online life, and IP addresses can place that person in a city or a household network at the time they were writing. For parents, the record is a useful prompt for a conversation rather than a password reset.
Young writers often reuse the same handle across fan communities, games and social apps, and a username that appeared in this file alongside a birth date and location is easy to search.

Checking where that handle is still in use, and whether any of those accounts link back to a real name or school, is a more meaningful step than changing a password that bcrypt already protected well.

background: In April 2020, Indonesia's largest online store Tokopedia suffered a data breach . The incident resulted in 15M rows of data being posted to a popular hacking forum. An additional 76M rows were later provided to HIBP in July 2020. In total, the data included over 71M unique email addresses alongside names, genders, birth dates and passwords stored as SHA2-384 hashes.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 71,443,698 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

editorial: Seventy-one million accounts at Indonesia's largest online marketplace. At that share of a national population a breach stops behaving like a corporate incident and starts behaving like a demographic dataset, names, genders and dates of birth for a substantial part of the country's online public, in one file, freely circulating.
The passwords were stored as SHA2-384 hashes, and the number in that name does more harm than good. SHA-2 is not a broken algorithm; it is the wrong kind of algorithm for this job.

It is built to be fast, and for password storage speed is the defect, the whole point of bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 is to be deliberately, tunably slow, so that an attacker with the file cannot test billions of guesses a second. A reassuring hash name is one of the most reliable ways to be wrong about password security.
Assume anything short or guessable in that file was recovered years ago, and change it anywhere it was reused.

The other half of the record never expires and never gets rotated: a name, a gender and a date of birth do not change, and a date of birth is one of the three details call centres still accept as proof that the person on the line is who they say they are.

The record describes two releases: 15 million rows posted to a forum in April 2020 and a further 76 million rows provided to HIBP in July. That pattern, a smaller public sample followed by a much larger private dataset, is common when data is being sold. The sample proves the seller has the goods, and the full file circulates among buyers.

People who checked their address in April 2020 and found nothing may have appeared only in the later, larger set. For Indonesian users, the practical risk is the one most marketplace breaches share: fake seller messages, fake order problems and fake promotions that use a real name.

Marketplace accounts may hold saved payment methods and wallet balances, so the account itself is worth protecting with a unique password and the strongest sign-in option the app offers, independently of whether the old password was ever cracked.

background: In October 2019, security researchers Vinny Troia and Bob Diachenko identified an unprotected Elasticsearch server holding 1.2 billion records of personal data . The exposed data included an index indicating it was sourced from data enrichment company People Data Labs (PDL) and contained 622 million unique email addresses.

The server was not owned by PDL and it's believed a customer failed to properly secure the database. Exposed information included email addresses, phone numbers, social media profiles and job history data.
how: In October 2019, security researchers Vinny Troia and Bob Diachenko identified an unprotected Elasticsearch server holding 1.2 billion records of personal data .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 622,161,052 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Geographic locations, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Social media profiles.
editorial: Nobody in this file signed up for anything. Data enrichment companies do not collect from you; they buy, scrape and merge from everywhere else, then sell a composite profile to businesses that want to know more about the people already in their own database. The 622 million people here were the product, not the customers.

The detail that makes it worse is where it was found. The exposed server was not the enrichment company's, it belonged to one of its customers, who had left an Elasticsearch instance on the open internet with no password.

So the data was assembled by one company, sold to a second, and exposed by the second, and there was no point in that chain at which any of the 622 million people could have been asked or told. That chain is the reason this record is worth reading even though the fields look mundane.

Name, employer, job title, phone number, location and social profiles is a background check, and it is the raw material for convincing approaches that appear to come from a colleague or a recruiter. If you want to understand how the industry that built it works, the guide on how data brokers turn a leak into a profile covers it.

The record credits two named security researchers with finding the server, which is how a large share of the exposures in this archive come to light: not through a company detecting a problem, but through someone outside scanning for open databases and reporting what they find.

The same scanning is done by criminals, and the record cannot say whether anyone else reached the server before the researchers did. Data enrichment profiles are also refreshed and resold, so the details in this 2019 file may have been corrected and re-circulated through other products since.

Opting out of the larger enrichment and people-data companies, under the privacy laws that give you that right, reduces what appears in the next leak. It does nothing for this one, but this one is not the last.

The incident exposed tens of millions of records of largely corporate contact data containing 17.8M unique email addresses, along with phone numbers, employers, job titles and geographic locations including state, city and postcode.

outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 17,838,396 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

editorial: LimeLeads sold B2B marketing leads, so, like many data brokers in this archive, most of the 17.8 million addresses in it belong to people who never dealt with the company. Their work email, direct phone number, employer, job title and location were compiled and sold for cold outreach, then left on an Elasticsearch server with no password.

An unsecured Elasticsearch database is one of the most familiar causes of data exposure and one of the least excusable. It is not a sophisticated attack; it is a database answering anyone who asks, and automated scanners that look for open servers find them quickly. The company is now defunct.

The data is not: copies of leads databases are resold and merged long after the original seller has gone. Breached in 2019 and added to Have I Been Pwned in 2026, this set is a reminder that "old" corporate contact data stays useful as long as people keep their jobs and phone numbers.

If you are in it, the realistic consequence is more targeted cold calls and spear phishing at work, not account takeover. It is also a reason to opt out of the B2B data brokers that keep selling the same records. The geographic fields are more precise than most corporate contact data, down to state, city and postcode.

Combined with a job title and employer, that narrows a record to one office, which is useful to anyone planning an in-person pretext, such as a courier who needs a signature or a visitor claiming to be from IT, as well as to phone fraud.

For most people that remains an unlikely use, but it is the reason security teams treat leaked lead lists as a reconnaissance resource rather than as spam. The seven-year gap between the 2019 breach and the 2026 HIBP date is long even for this archive, and it shows how slowly leaked lead data surfaces publicly.

Companies whose staff appear in it can use the HIBP domain search to see how many of their addresses are included, which is a quick way to judge how much of the organisation chart is already in circulation and which teams should expect targeted calls.

background: In May 2013, the Russian-language hacking forum YouHack suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data . The breach exposed 107k forum members' email addresses, usernames, IP addresses and MD5 password hashes, most of which were unsalted.
Forum posts also contained email address and password pairs belonging to other victims, bringing the total to 7.2M unique email addresses.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 7,160,849 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, IP addresses, Passwords, Usernames.
editorial: A hacking forum getting hacked is a familiar story, but the numbers here are the interesting part. YouHack had about 107,000 members. This entry lists 7.2 million email addresses. The difference is the forum's own content: members posted email and password pairs taken from other victims, so most people in this set were never members. They were the material being traded.

That makes it two breaches in one. For the members, the exposure is their email, username, IP address and an MD5 password hash, mostly unsalted, which modern hardware reverses quickly for anything but a long random password. For everyone else, it means a password of theirs was already circulating among people who collect them by 2013. Old does not mean harmless.

Password reuse is a habit, and a password from 2013 is often a close variant of one still in use today. If your address is here, check whether you still use that password, or a pattern built from it, anywhere. Our password leak check guide explains how to test it without sending the password itself.

The gap between the breach date and the HIBP date is one of the longest in this archive. The forum was breached in May 2013 and the data was added in November 2026, more than thirteen years later, as part of a larger redistributed corpus.

That timeline is typical of old forum breaches: the data circulates privately for years, is bundled into compilations, and only becomes searchable when one of those compilations reaches someone who reports it. For the forum's own members, the IP addresses are the field with the longest tail.

A member of a Russian-language hacking forum in 2013 may have very good reasons not to want that association surfacing now, and an IP address from that period can still be tied to an ISP and a region. Anyone who used the forum under a username they still use elsewhere should treat that handle as linked to this record.
